ref: #page-header-bg > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > h1
subject: CONTATO
message: The text "CONTATO" has at most 2.95:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #febd7d…#d88201), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an image in the element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 3:1 for large text.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the page's h1 'CONTATO', white bold text about 51 px tall (large text, 3:1 required) over the page header photo (010.jpg, alt="", no overlay; the header's only background colour is #000 under the image). In the screenshot the whole word sits on orange to light-orange parts of the photo. I measured the background pixels in the heading's box: white against them gives a median of about 2.0:1, 90% of pixels under 2.65:1, and only about 2% (at the darker left edge) reach 3:1, up to 3.2:1. So the claim (at most 2.95:1, background #febd7d to #d88201, below 3:1 for large text) holds in substance; its maximum is a robust value rather than the extreme pixel. elementFails yes: the text fails 1.4.3 against its background, and the claim names that failure. The live HTML has the same header image, the same h1 and no overlay, so captureDiffers no.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the page's h1 "CONTATO": white (#ffffff), 51px Oswald bold, so large text that needs 3:1. It sits on the page-header photograph (an img, 010.jpg, scaled to cover the 500px header) of an orange-lit violin with a white glare. I looked for a way it could pass and found none. The live HTML has data-parallax=0, so the image does not move with scroll. It has no overlay over the image, and neither the inline styles nor Salient's style.css put a text-shadow on the page-header h1. I measured the screenshot's pixels within the h1's glyph area myself. Column by column, the median background contrast with white runs from 2.65:1 under the "C" down to 1.65:1 under the final "O", where the glare is. Only an isolated corner pixel reaches 3.2:1. This agrees with Rampa's 2.95:1 best and 1.64:1 worst. The snapshot keeps the class "not-loaded" on the header, but the screenshot shows the image rendered, which is the final state users see. The live page has the same image, header and heading, so the capture matches it. The text fails 1.4.3, and the claim names that failure.

html: <input id="wpcf7-6b01bb53e1d95-field" class="wpcf7-form-control wpcf7-text" type="text" name="honey-196" value="" autocomplete="new-password" tabindex="1000" data-cf7apps-tabindex="1000">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the Contact Form 7 honeypot field (name honey-196), a spam trap. Its wrapper span is visually hidden with the sr-only pattern (inline style position:absolute; width:1px; height:1px; overflow:hidden; clip:rect(0,0,0,0)); the snapshot gives the wrapper 1x1 px bounds and the label textVisible false, and the screenshot shows nothing at the field's position below the reCAPTCHA. claimTrue yes: the label 'Please leave this field empty.' exists and its text does not show; nothing visible labels the field (the ENVIAR button is about 170 px away). elementFails no: the field itself is just as invisible as its label, it is not content that asks the user for input (it must be left empty), and it carries a programmatic label that tells screen reader users exactly that, so 3.3.2 is met. The rule demanded a visible label for a field that is not presented visually. Other issues: tabindex=1000 puts this invisible field first in the tab order with no visible focus (2.4.3/2.4.7), and the English label on a pt-BR page is a 3.1.2 matter. The live HTML has the same markup and inline style, so captureDiffers no.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the Contact Form 7 honeypot input (name honey-196), an anti-spam trap. Its wrapper span is visually hidden with an inline screen-reader-only style (position:absolute; 1px by 1px; overflow:hidden; clip:rect(0,0,0,0)). The snapshot gives the wrapper as 1x1, and the screenshot shows nothing under the reCAPTCHA where the input's bounds fall. The claim is true of the capture: the label "Please leave this field empty." exists and is associated, but its text does not show (textVisible false). But the field does not show either. Sighted users are never shown a field to fill in, and screen reader users hear the label, which tells them what to do. Understanding 3.3.2 is about fields and controls "that expect user input". This one expects none: it is meant to stay empty. A visible label is not required for a control that is not presented visually, so the element does not fail 3.3.2. The rule asks for visible label text without checking that the field itself is visually hidden, which is stricter than the criterion. The real problem here is a different one: tabindex=1000 puts this invisible field early in the keyboard tab order (2.4.3 focus order and 2.4.7 focus visible), and the claim does not name that. The live HTML fetched today has the same hidden wrapper, label and tabindex, so the capture matches what users receive.

ref: #logo > img:nth-of-type(1)

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header logo image (Logo.png, the dark version) inside the link #logo to the home page, with alt="Orquestra Ouro Preto". The crop shows the logo mark and the words ORQUESTRA OURO PRETO with a small tagline MAESTRO RODRIGO TOFFOLO. As the only meaningful content of a link, its alternative names the organisation and so the destination (the home page titled 'Orquestra Ouro Preto - Excelencia e Versatilidade'), which is what H30 asks for (its example uses the site's name). Leaving out the small tagline does not change the link's purpose, so the image meets 1.1.1 and Rampa was right to report nothing. elementFails no. The live HTML has the same image and alt (plus the white starting logo with the same alt), so captureDiffers no. Side notes outside this criterion: the snapshot's link name is the text of a PageSpeed <script> inside the link, which browsers exclude from the name (a collector artefact), and the two logo images with the same alt may make the link name repeat.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header logo image (alt "Orquestra Ouro Preto"), the first of two images that make up the home link #logo; the logo shows the OP monogram and the words "Orquestra Ouro Preto" with a small "Maestro Rodrigo Toffolo" tagline. As a control's alternative it names the destination, the orchestra's home page (titled "Orquestra Ouro Preto - Excelência e Versatilidade"), the same way H30's "Smallville Times" example names the site, so it describes the link's purpose and meets 1.1.1; leaving out the tagline does not stop users from knowing where the link goes. The snapshot's own link name (the text of a PageSpeed script inside the link) is a collector artefact; the browser's accessibility tree gives "Orquestra Ouro Preto Orquestra Ouro Preto", repeated because the second logo image has the same alt. That repetition is redundant, not a 1.1.1 failure of this image. The live HTML fetched today has the same two images with the same alt, so the capture does not differ on this point. Rampa was right to report nothing.

ref: #menu-item-5753 > a

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the main-menu item 'Apresentacao' (href="#", aria-haspopup=true, aria-expanded=false), the parent of a nested submenu list (Orquestra, Maestro, Revista, OOP Experience, Eventos) in the same list item. Its purpose is to open the 'Apresentacao' (about) section of the menu, which its text, its popup state and its list item with the nested list (H81 context) make clear. No other link shares its name. It meets 2.4.4, and Rampa was right to report nothing. Using a link with href="#" as a menu button is a role question under 4.1.2, not 2.4.4. The live HTML has the same markup, so captureDiffers no.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the main-menu item "Apresentação": a link with href="#", aria-haspopup=true and aria-expanded=false, which opens a submenu. Its parent list item holds the submenu links (Orquestra, Maestro, Revista OOP Experience, Eventos), and that list item counts as its programmatically determined context. The browser exposes it as having a menu popup and being collapsed. The name, the state and that list item together make its purpose clear: it opens the Apresentação section's submenu. So it meets 2.4.4. The only other link with that name is in the off-canvas mobile menu, which is hidden from the accessibility tree; it has the same href and does the same job, so no shared-name problem arises. A link with href="#" used as a menu toggle might raise a 4.1.2 role question, but that is not 2.4.4. The live HTML has the same markup. Rampa was right to report nothing.

ref: html > body > main > section:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > div > img
subject: Card image cap
message: The text alternative "Card image cap" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: html > body > main > section:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > div > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Image uel-estude-na-uel.png at the top of the 'Vida na UEL' card link 'Estude na UEL', alt='Card image cap' (the Bootstrap template placeholder). The crop and the screenshot show a white line icon of a book on green. The alt describes nothing the image shows, so the claim holds. Placeholder text isn't a text alternative (F30). The icon repeats the link text and should have alt='', but its placeholder is read as part of the link name instead ('Card image cap Estude na UEL'). The live HTML is the same. The claim points at that defect: fails 1.1.1.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Decorative white line icon (a book) at the top of the green 'Vida na UEL' card link 'Estude na UEL', with alt="Card image cap", the Bootstrap placeholder text. The live page still serves the same alt, so captureDiffers is no. The crop shows only the icon; nothing in it is a 'card image cap', so the claim is true of the capture. Skeptic check: the icon is redundant with the link text, so the right alternative is null (H2/H67), but the placeholder is not ignorable by assistive technology and is read into the link name ('Card image cap Estude na UEL' in Chrome's tree). That is F30 (placeholder text as an alternative) and F39 (non-null alt on an image that should be ignored), so the element fails 1.1.1 whether the icon is read as decorative or informative. The claim that the alternative does not describe the image points at that defect in good faith: true_positive.

subject: link
message: The name the browser computes for this link is only an icon-font glyph (U+F107, a private use character from CSS), which screen readers do not read. Give it a text name (aria-label or visually hidden text) and hide the icon (aria-hidden).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The scroll-down arrow in the hero is <a onclick="scrollInto('sectionSocialMedia')"> holding only a Font Awesome fa-angle-down icon (visible as the round arrow at about x 610, y 696 in the screenshot). ref: #vlibras-access-wrapper >>> div > img
subject: hidden vlibras-popup.webp
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (inside aria-hidden="true"), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "The image says "acessível com VLibras"".

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is img#vlibras-popup (alt 'Acessível com VLibras') inside the VLibras widget's shadow root, next to the VLibras button. claimTrue: in the capture it is inside #vlibras-access-wrapper with aria-hidden='true', so it is hidden from assistive technology. The image does say 'Acessível com VLibras', and no surrounding text says it; the sibling button's aria-label says much the same but is hidden too. elementFails: the VLibras plugin (vlibras.gov.br/app/vlibras-plugin.js) never sets aria-hidden. In the snapshot, app-root carries aria-hidden='true' too: the Angular Material dialog hides every sibling of its overlay from assistive technology while the WhatsApp modal is open, the standard modal pattern, and removes it on close. Outside that state the image is exposed with a fitting alt, which meets 1.1.1. Even with the modal open, the image is not displayed at rest. The plugin's CSS keeps #vlibras-access at 40px with the button absolutely positioned above the image, so the image only shows when the widget widens to 200px on hover or focus. The screenshot shows only the hand button at 10,380, and the crop is the image's own source, not what is on screen. Background content hidden while a modal is open does not make this image fail 1.1.1. The odd part is that the VLibras button floats above the backdrop while hidden, which is a 4.1.2/1.3.1 matter for the button, not this image. captureDiffers: the capture faithfully shows the modal-open state that first-time visitors also get, and nothing else differs. False positive: the checker did not know the aria-hidden came from the modal and that the image sits under the button.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the VLibras widget's pop-up image (vlibras-popup.webp, an image of the words 'Acessível com VLibras'), which only slides out from behind the VLibras button on hover or keyboard focus. Its alt is 'Acessível com VLibras', which matches what it says, so it has an adequate text alternative. The aria-hidden that the claim cites does not come from the image or from VLibras (the live vlibras-plugin.js sets none on #vlibras-access-wrapper). Angular Material's modal dialog sets aria-hidden='true' on every sibling of its overlay container while the WhatsApp promotion dialog is open (app-root has it as well) and removes it when the dialog closes, which is the usual way to hide background content behind a modal. claimTrue: hidden is true in the capture, but the claim that it conveys something the surrounding text does not say is false, since the sibling button's name ('Conteúdo acessível em Libras usando o VLibras Widget...') says the same. elementFails: no for 1.1.1. The widget showing above the backdrop while hidden from assistive technology could be a 4.1.2 or 1.3.1 question about the button, not a missing text alternative. captureDiffers: the live page's bundle and plugin match the capture, and the dialog state is one users also get on load. The checker did not know the hiding came from a temporary modal state, and did not credit the matching alt.

ref: #mat-dialog-0 > main > section:nth-of-type(1) > ex-tag > button > div > span
subject: WhatsApp
message: The text "WhatsApp" has at most 2.17:1 contrast with what is behind it (#2fbd5d on #247865…#237864), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the label 'WhatsApp' of the tag (ex-tag, type icon, extended state success) at the top of the WhatsApp promo dialog (#mat-dialog-0). The page opens that dialog on load, and it sits above the backdrop, so it is not dimmed. claimTrue: the snapshot's pixelContrast gives foreground #2fbd5d (CSS), background #247865/#237864, 2.17:1, 12.25px weight 500, axe reason bgGradient. I recomputed 2.17:1, and the screenshot pixels under the text are #247865/#237865 with the glyphs no lighter than #2cab60. elementFails: it is normal-size text, so 4.5:1 applies, and the crop shows faint green on teal. None of the exceptions holds. The tag is not disabled: it uses the ex-tag--success styling, not ex-tag--disabled, so it is not an inactive component. It is not decoration either, since it labels the dialog's topic. One could read the word as a brand name under the logotype exception, but this is the design system's success-coloured tag text in the site's typeface (Poppins), not a logo, so I do not apply it. captureDiffers: I could not render the SPA (curl returns only the Angular shell), but the current bundle has the same modal template (ex-wa-modal with an ex-tag labelled WhatsApp in the success state) and the same tag colours. A first-time visitor gets the same dialog, so I found no difference that touches the claim. True positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'WhatsApp' label of the tag at the top of the WhatsApp promotion dialog (12.25px, weight 500, normal-size text). claimTrue: the screenshot shows the text and border at #2fbd5d on a tinted teal of #247865, about 2.17:1, as stated. elementFails: the live CSS confirms it: .ex-tag--success sets color var(--ex-border-and-text-success) = #2fbd5d on --ex-bg-success = #2fbd5d33 laid over the dialog's linear-gradient(#256464 to #0b7675), so the text is well under 4.5:1. I looked for exemptions: the tag is neither disabled (no ex-tag--disabled) nor in button mode, and it is not styled as inactive, so the inactive-component exception does not apply; it labels the channel, so it is not pure decoration (repeating the heading does not exempt it); it is plain text in the site's Poppins font, not the WhatsApp logotype, so the logotype exception does not hold up. The dialog was fully rendered (its white text measures 6.1 to 6.6:1 on the opaque gradient), so this is not an animation artefact. captureDiffers: the live bundle has the same dialog and colour tokens; the dialog opens on the home page, so users receive this text.

ref: html > body > app-root > app-home > main > ex-page-container > article > section > div > ex-core-search > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > section > div > section > ex-core-speech-to-text > section > ex-action-button > button
subject: Permissão de acesso ao microfone não concedida
message: The icon of this button ("Permissão de acesso ao microfone não concedida") has at most 2.51:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#939cad on #f4f4f4). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <button _ngcontent-fql-c262="" fxlayout="column" fxlayoutalign="center center" type="button" class="mat-tooltip-trigger ex-action-button--disabled ex-action-button ex-border-primary ex-br-4xl ex-bw-md ex-bs-solid ex-action-button--standard ex-action-button--lg ng-star-inserted" aria-label="Permissão de acesso ao microfone não concedida" role="button" style="flex-direction: column; box-sizing: border-box; display: flex; place-content: center; align-items: center;">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the voice-search button (ex-core-speech-to-text) in the search bar, in its 'permissionDenied' state: icon fa-microphone-slash, class ex-action-button--disabled, aria-label 'Permissão de acesso ao microfone não concedida'. claimTrue: the snapshot records the icon colour #939cad from CSS on #f4f4f4 and 2.51:1, which I recomputed; the screenshot shows #a6a6a6 there only because the WhatsApp dialog's backdrop (rgba(0,0,0,.32)) dims it, and 244 x 0.68 gives that grey, so the undimmed background is #f4f4f4. The icon is all the button shows. elementFails: the site's bundle (main.61fad181cecd444c56b6.js) shows this is an inactive control. startRecording runs only when state is 'ready', so in this state activating the button does nothing. The --disabled class gives it the design system's disabled colour (--ex-text-neutral-primary-disabled) and cursor:not-allowed, and its tooltip says why. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts inactive user interface components, those not available for user interaction, so the 3:1 requirement does not apply here. It does fail elsewhere: being focusable and exposed as a normal button without a disabled or aria-disabled state is a 4.1.2 matter. captureDiffers: the component starts in permissionDenied for every visitor and stays there when the user refuses the microphone, has none, or has not answered the prompt. Users who grant permission get the 'ready' icon instead, which this claim is not about. The aria-hidden on the button comes from the open WhatsApp modal, which real first-time visitors also get. False positive: the rule applied 3:1 to a component the criterion exempts.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the voice-search button in the search bar (ex-core-speech-to-text), showing a slashed microphone icon. claimTrue: with the dialog backdrop removed the icon is #939cad on #f4f4f4, about 2.5:1, and the screenshot agrees once the 32% black backdrop is factored out (#636975 on #a6a6a6); the icon is all the button shows. elementFails: the live bundle sets exDisabled whenever the state is permissionDenied (also error and loading), which adds ex-action-button--disabled (disabled grey colour, cursor:not-allowed), and startRecording only runs in the ready state, so in this state the button is an inactive component, which 1.4.11 exempts ('except for inactive components'). It is not programmatically disabled (no disabled or aria-disabled, still focusable), which is a 4.1.2 matter, not a 1.4.11 one; in the ready state the icon uses --ex-base-primary, which this claim is not about. captureDiffers: the automated browser got no microphone permission; real browsers start in the same permissionDenied state, ask for the microphone on load, and stay disabled until access is granted, so users receive this same state; the live bundle matches. The rule applied 3:1 to a component the criterion exempts.

ref: #navbarNavAltMarkup > div > a > img

message: The text alternative "Logo" is a file name or a placeholder.

patch.ref: #navbarNavAltMarkup > div > a > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header SBIm logotype (the crop shows the image of text 'SBIm Sociedade Brasileira de Imunizações') is the only content of a link to home, with alt="Logo". 'Logo' is a generic placeholder word: it names neither the society shown in the image nor where the link goes, so it fails H30 (the alternative of an image that is a link's only content must describe the link's function) and is the kind of placeholder F30 names. The claim's 'placeholder' names that defect (it is not the file name, but the sentence says 'or'). The live server-rendered HTML has the same img and alt, so the capture matches.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header SBIm logo (logo-sbim.svg) is the only content of the link to home, with alt="Logo"; the snapshot's accessibility name of the link is just "Logo", and the link has no aria-label or title. "Logo" is a generic placeholder word, like F30's "image" or "picture": put in place of the image it neither names SBIm nor says the link goes to the home page, which H30 requires for an image that is a link's only content. I looked for a way out (other text in the link, an aria-label, a title) and found none. The live server HTML has the same , so the capture matches. The claim names the real defect.

That alternative states something the image does not show and adds a wrong word to the link's name ('Telefone Rua Luís Coelho...'), so it does not serve the purpose of the image. skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the icon in the footer's address link (href to Google Maps). Its src is marker-pin-white.svg, and the crop shows a map pin, but its alt is "Telefone", copied from the phone item above it (phone-white.svg, also alt "Telefone"). The browser computes the link's name as "Telefone Rua Luís Coelho, 308 – 5º andar...", so screen reader users are told this is a phone item when it is an address. As skeptic I asked whether the icon could count as decorative, which would make its alt harmless. It cannot: a decorative image would need a null alt, and this one gives false information. Its alternative does not serve the image's purpose, so it fails 1.1.1 (F30's test). The live HTML has the same markup. The claim names the defect.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The footer badge (the crop shows the Vaccine Safety Net logo, 'vaccine safety net') is a plain image, not a link, with src vsn-logo.png and alt="vsn-logo", the file's base name. That is F30's failure (a file name used as the text alternative). If the badge were taken as redundant with the sentence beside it ('Site integrante da Vaccine Safety Net (VSN)...'), it would need a null alt to be ignored; either way the filename alt that screen readers announce fails 1.1.1. The live HTML has the same alt.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the Vaccine Safety Net badge in the footer's bottom band (vsn-logo.png, alt="vsn-logo"). It is not a link, and it sits right beside the text "Site integrante da Vaccine Safety Net (VSN) – uma rede global de sites validados pela Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS)". The alt is the file's base name, so the claim's sentence is true. But F30 only fails file names "that are not valid text alternatives in their own right", and its test asks whether the text can replace the image without losing information. Read aloud, "vsn-logo" says it is the VSN logo, and the next sentence spells VSN out, so nothing is lost. The badge is arguably redundant with that text, too. I lean towards a pass, but auditors split on file-name-shaped alts like this one. The live HTML is identical.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: A disabled, checked checkbox in the cookie consent banner ('Este site armazena cookies em seu computador...'), labelled 'Não opcionais' beside a second checkbox 'Estatísticas'. A checkbox takes no typed entry; its label names the option, the cookie category that cannot be turned off, and inside the cookie banner that describes its purpose, which is what 2.4.6 asks. 'Does not say what to enter' does not fit the control. The banner appears in the screenshot, and the live page injects the same consent block from its scripts.

skeptic.label: false_positive

It is a checkbox, so there is nothing to "enter". In its context the label names the category of cookies the box stands for (the non-optional ones, which cannot be unticked), and that is the topic or purpose 2.4.6 asks a label to describe. The claim holds the checkbox to a text-field standard that 2.4.6 does not set. The live page's cookie script builds the same markup (), and the screenshot shows the banner.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Newsletter sign-up field under 'Receba as principais notícias do RN': it collects the user's own e-mail address, a purpose in the WCAG Input Purposes list (email). The input is type=text, name=newsletter, autocomplete=off, so nothing programmatically identifies that purpose. Understanding 1.3.5 says that even when authors want to stop autofill, input purposes still need to be programmatically determinable. So the field fails 1.3.5 for exactly the reason the claim gives. The live HTML has the same markup.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Newsletter sign-up field: type=text, name=newsletter, autocomplete=off, placeholder 'E-mail...', next to 'Assinar gratuitamente'. It collects the user's own email address, a purpose listed in the Input Purposes section ('email'). Nothing identifies that purpose programmatically: autocomplete is 'off' and the type is not email, so the field fails H98's test. A possible defence is that the ACT rule 73f2c2 leaves 'off' out of its applicability. That rule only checks token validity, though, and does not show the purpose is determinable. The live HTML still has autocomplete="off" and type="text". The claim names exactly this failure.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > article:nth-of-type(4) > a > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
message: The text alternative "Foto: Leobark Rodrigues/Secom/TSE" describes something the image does not show.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Thumbnail inside the teaser link for 'Relatório da PF tem diálogos de Vorcaro sobre Mendonça...'. The crop shows a man in judicial robes at a bench (the minister the story is about). Its alt is only a photo credit, 'Foto: Leobark Rodrigues/Secom/TSE'. The image is not the link's only content (the headline is also in the link), so R2 does not apply. Treated as informative, the credit is not an alternative to the picture: it does not convey who or what is shown (F30). Treated as decorative next to the headline, it needed a null alt and instead adds the credit to the link name (F39). Either way it fails 1.1.1. Read in good faith, 'describes something the image does not show' names that defect, and the credit is literally not shown in the image. The live HTML still has the same alt.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: News thumbnail inside a card link that also holds the headline 'Relatório da PF tem diálogos de Vorcaro sobre Mendonça...'. It is not an image-only link, so R2 does not apply. The crop shows a minister in robes at a court bench. The alt is only a photo credit, 'Foto: Leobark Rodrigues/Secom/TSE', which identifies nothing shown in the image. Read as informative, the image needs at least a descriptive identification; read as redundant with the headline, it needs a null alt (H2/F39). The credit is neither, so it is not a text alternative (F30's sense), and the image fails 1.1.1 either way. The claim that the alternative describes something the image does not show points at that mismatch in good faith. The live HTML still gives this image the same alt.

subject: VTEX
message: The link text "VTEX" is shared by 13 links that lead to 7 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

patch.ref: #cookiescript_reportwrap > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > table > tbody > tr:nth-of-type(2) > td:nth-of-type(2) > div > a
patch.after: Política de Privacidade da VTEX

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: A 'VTEX' link in the Provider / Domínio column of the strictly-necessary cookie table (row 2, cell text 'www.polishop.com.br VTEX', href https://vtex.com/br-pt/privacy/). Context under the rubric: its cell (provider + cookie domain) and the column header 'Provider / Domínio'; no title, no aria-describedby, the cookie name is in a plain td (not a row header), and the heading before it ('Marcas' in the sidebar) is the same for all. claimTrue yes: the capture has 13 links named VTEX with 7 distinct hrefs, and the cells with the same domain text are identical contexts. elementFails no by R1: I opened all seven VTEX hrefs of the table on 2026-11-21: each redirects to www.vtex.com/(pt-br|en-us|en)/... and answers HTTP 404 with the same ~29 KB not-found template (the vtex.com home page and its real privacy notice at /en-us/trust/general-external-privacy-notice answer 200 to the same client), so every VTEX link of the table, terms-and-conditions included, lands on the same not-found page and they resolve to equivalent resources. Nothing visible tells a sighted user that one VTEX link leads somewhere different from another either: each is the provider entry of a cookie row. So the shared name does not fail 2.4.4; the link text with the Provider header gives its purpose (the provider's page). captureDiffers no: At capture the cookie details panel (#cookiescript_cookietablewrap) is collapsed: CookieScript marks it inert with opacity 0 and height 0 (the snapshot's CDP data lists its cells as ignored for inertElement), and it opens when the user activates 'Mostrar detalhes'; the content is the same once opened, and the live CookieScript file (cdn.cookie-script.com/s/366bff387d0c0ec4b071dcadb6e609d0.js, read 2026-11-21) carries the same rows, so the capture does not differ in a way that matters. False positive: Rampa counted distinct URLs without reading the destinations.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: 'VTEX' provider link (row checkout.vtex.com, href /br-pt/privacy/). The link sits in the 'Provider / Domínio' column of the Cookie-Script cookie report (strict category table), which is collapsed and inert at load and shown after 'Mostrar detalhes'. Its rubric context is the link text, its cell ('VTEX www.polishop.com.br') and the column header; the cookie name sits in another td, not a header cell. So it is in one set with the other 'VTEX' links of the same domain group, whose hrefs differ (privacy URLs in several locales plus /us-en/terms-and-conditions/), and the claim's count (13 links, 7 hrefs) is exact for the capture. Skeptic check on the destinations: every one of these VTEX URLs (br-pt/privacy, br-pt/privacy-policy, en/privacy, en/privacy-policy, privacy-policy/en, www.vtex.com/privacy-policy, us-en/terms-and-conditions) now redirects to VTEX's new locale paths and answers HTTP 404; rendered in a real browser each shows the identical '404 Page Not Found' page (VTEX moved its legal pages under /trust/). Under R1 every pair in the set therefore resolves to the same or an equivalent resource, so the link meets 2.4.4 on this ground (the dead links are a defect, but not a 2.4.4 one). Checked about 2.5 hours after Rampa's read; nothing suggests the old paths were live then. The live Cookie-Script config carries the same 13 VTEX links and hrefs, so the capture matches. Rampa never read the destinations and judged from differing URLs.

A checkbox takes no entry: the label names the cookie category that checking it consents to, so the sentence that it 'does not say what to enter' does not hold of the capture. In that dialog the label describes the control's purpose, which is what 2.4.6 asks; the details panel also explains 'Targeting cookies are used to identify visitors between different websites'. It meets 2.4.6. The live CookieScript file (cdn.cookie-script.com, linked from the live page) still renders the same label for cookiescript_category_targeting, so the capture does not differ. skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Targeting' checkbox in the CookieScript consent dialog. Its label element reads 'Targeting', and CSS uppercases it to 'TARGETING'. The claim's sentence is literally true: the label does not say what to enter. But this is a checkbox, so nothing is entered. 2.4.6 asks only that a label describe the control's topic or purpose. Here the dialog is headed 'This website uses cookies', and the checkbox sits in a group with 'Strictly necessary', 'Performance' and 'Unclassified'. In that context 'Targeting' clearly names the choice: consent to targeting cookies. Understanding 2.4.6 does not ask for long labels, and asking a label to say what to enter is a 3.3.2-style instruction requirement applied to the wrong kind of control. The live page loads the same CookieScript script, which serves the same checkbox and label, and the screenshot shows the dialog as the snapshot does. So the capture does not differ, and the element meets 2.4.6.

ref: #mh-search
subject: Search
message: The text "Search" has at most 3.10:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #009cdb), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The 'Search' button of the myhome.ie property widget in the sidebar. The widget's live stylesheet (media.myhome.ie/cdn/widget/styles.css) sets #mh-search {background:#009cdb; color:#fff; font-weight:bold}, and the screenshot shows white bold text on that blue. White on #009cdb is 3.10:1; at 13px bold this is not large text (needs 14pt bold), so 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1. The claim states the colours and ratio correctly. Third-party widget, but it is part of the page.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Search button of the embedded myhome property-search widget in the sidebar: white bold 13px text on a #009cdb button. The crop of the screenshot shows exactly that, and the computed ratio is 3.10:1. 13px bold is not large text (that needs 14pt bold, about 18.7px), so 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1. I looked for a reason it passes: the colours are solid, not an anti-aliasing artefact, there is no incidental or logotype exception, and the widget is in the page's own DOM (not an iframe), so it is part of the page's content. My fetch of the live raw HTML does not render the script-injected widget, but the capture is a fully styled browser render and nothing suggests a different style for users. The claim names the failure.

subject: facebook
message: The icon of this link ("facebook") has at most 2.71:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#9d9d9c on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Icon-only link 'facebook' (grey square with the 'f' knocked out) in the sidebar FOLLOW ECHO block. The live page still renders the same SVG with .st0{fill:#9d9d9c} and only switches to brand colours on hover (.mobile-apps ...:hover path{Fill:...}), and the screenshot shows grey squares with white glyphs on white. Grey #9d9d9c against white is 2.71:1, both for the square against the page and for the white glyph inside it, below the 3:1 that 1.4.11 asks of a graphical object that is all that identifies a control. The logo exemption does not cover a low-contrast variant chosen by the author (brand blue only on hover). The claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Icon-only facebook link: the SVG path is a filled #9d9d9c square with the 'f' cut out, so the glyph is white on grey and the tile is grey on white, both 2.71:1, under 1.4.11's 3:1 for the only visual identifying the control. The live HTML serves the same inline SVG with the same .st0 fill #9d9d9c, and the screenshot is a fully styled render, so the capture matches what users receive. I looked for a way out: the FOLLOW ECHO text above the row labels the group but does not tell the links apart, so the icon is still the only visual identification of this control. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos on the assumption that brand guidelines dictate their colours, but says a logo is not exempt when the author chose the low-contrast variant; a neutral grey rendition is the site's own styling, not a colour these brands require. The claim names the failure.

ref: #more-click-menu
subject: MORE
message: The link text "MORE" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

patch.ref: #more-click-menu
patch.after: More navigation options

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: 'MORE' in the main navigation, href='#', a hover/click toggle for a dropdown. Its list item (part of its programmatically determined context under this rubric) contains the dropdown's links: Advertise with us, Mini Marathon 2026, Find a House, Find a Job, Competitions, Photosales, Subscribe, epaper, Contact Us and so on, so what the control reveals can be determined from its context and the claim that nothing around it tells is false. Exposing a menu toggle as a link without aria-expanded is a 4.1.2 matter, not 2.4.4. The live page has the same markup. Rampa had the list item text in its ancestors.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'MORE' item of the main navigation (href='#', a hover dropdown toggle). Its own list item, which the rubric counts as programmatically determined context, contains the dropdown's links (Advertise with us, Mini Marathon 2026, Find a House, Find a Job, Competitions ... Echo Sport Podcast), exposed in the accessibility tree. So the link text with its list item tells users it opens more site sections. The claim's 'nothing around it does' is false. Using a link rather than a button for a menu toggle is a 4.1.2 matter, not 2.4.4. The model had that list-item text in its context. The live HTML is the same.

skeptic.rationale: Main-navigation link 'Wow!' (shown as WOW!) to /wow/, a section whose page title is 'WoW - Echolive', in a list of section links (Cork News, Cork Sport, Cork Lives, Nostalgia...). skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Cork Lives teaser photo (file 'OthelloPic': people in costume by a stone building) inside a link whose visible text is the same headline quote the alt repeats: 'I left LA to be an actor in Cork ... I've always loved the rain!'. Literally, the alt is a quote, and LA and the rain are not in the picture, so the sentence holds. The skeptic's counter-reasons: the alt names the story's subject (the actress quoted, who appears to be in the cast photo); the image only supplements a link that already carries the same words; and duplicating the headline is a redundancy problem (H2 suggests a null alt), not something a 1.1.1 failure names. I lean to a pass, but auditors would reasonably split on whether a headline-as-alt that says nothing about the photo is an equivalent. The live homepage still serves the same image and alt.

ref: #custom-navbar-expand > div > nav > div:nth-of-type(1) > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > a
message: The link text "instagram" is shared by 3 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: Header social link, icon only, aria-label 'instagram', to https://www.instagram.com/echolive.ie/. The visible links with that name are this one, the sidebar 'Instagram' (same address plus ?hl=en) and the footer 'instagram' (same address); a fourth copy in the sub-navigation is hidden. ?hl=en only sets Instagram's interface language, so all resolve to the same profile (R1: same resource), and the sidebar and footer links are also told apart by their preceding headings (FOLLOW ECHO, Follow Us). So the claim's 'two different places' is false and the purpose, the site's Instagram account, is clear from the name: 2.4.4 is met. Rampa did not read the destinations. Live page has the same links.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header icon link named 'instagram' (fa icon, aria-label) to https://www.instagram.com/echolive.ie/. The snapshot has three such links in the accessibility tree (header, the FOLLOW ECHO sidebar 'Instagram', and the footer under 'Follow Us') plus a hidden subnav copy. Their only URL difference is that the sidebar adds '?hl=en', which just sets Instagram's interface language on the same @echolive.ie profile: the same or an equivalent resource under R1. The preceding headings also differ (none, FOLLOW ECHO, Follow Us), so they are not even one set. The claim that they lead to two different places is wrong; the link's purpose is clear. The model had the hrefs and misread a language parameter as a different destination. The live HTML has the same links.

ref: #wrapper > header > div:nth-of-type(6) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > a > img
subject: Trustpilot logo
message: The text alternative "Trustpilot logo" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: #wrapper > header > div:nth-of-type(6) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > a > img

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the Trustpilot rating badge in the header USP bar (image crop and screenshot: the word 'Excellent', 4.5 green stars and the Trustpilot logotype). It is the only content of a link to /customer-service/about-us/customer-reviews.html, a Cotton Traders page titled 'Cotton Traders Reviews' that embeds a Trustpilot review widget; the footer links to the same address as 'Trustpilot Reviews'. The link has no title, and its name comes only from alt='Trustpilot logo'. claimTrue yes: the image is all the link holds, and the alternative describes the picture as a logo without naming the reviews page. elementFails yes for 1.1.1: the alternative leaves out what the badge conveys (an 'Excellent', 4.5-star rating, shown as text in the image) and names the picture instead of the link's function, which H30 asks for. Uncertain because competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether the claim names that failure. 'Trustpilot', read as link text on a retailer's header, arguably lets users tell that the link leads to the store's Trustpilot reviews (R2's first test, and the site's own footer name for the page), so the destination point is borderline. The clearer defect is the omitted rating, which the claim does not mention. captureDiffers no: the live HTML has the same link, img, alt and href, the badge SVG (same dw8501b568 version) is static, and the screenshot shows the badge as captured.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header badge image (shows 'Excellent', 4.5 green stars and the Trustpilot mark), the only content of a link to /customer-service/about-us/customer-reviews.html; the link has no title or aria attributes, so its name is the alt 'Trustpilot logo'. claimTrue: as captured, the alt names the picture (a logo) and does not mention reviews or the destination page. elementFails: the image fails 1.1.1 at least because its text 'Excellent' and the star rating are not in the alternative, and 'logo' describes the image rather than the link's function (H30). But the claim's own reason is contestable: the destination is 'Cotton Traders Reviews', a page built around a Trustpilot review widget, and the site's footer link to the same URL reads 'Trustpilot Reviews', so 'Trustpilot' arguably names what the link leads to and, under R2's first test, many auditors would accept it as identifying the destination. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree about whether the failure the claim names holds, so the label is uncertain. captureDiffers: the live HTML (fetched 2026-11-21) has the same link, href, image and alt, and the screenshot is fully styled; no difference.

ref: #wrapper > header > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > form > div:nth-of-type(1) > input:nth-of-type(1)
subject: Search here...
message: The placeholder "Search here..." has a contrast of 3.36:1 with the field (#8c8c8c on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="text" class="js-search-input" name="q" value="" autocomplete="off" placeholder="Search here..." aria-label="Search here...">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field. Its placeholder 'Search here...' is its only visible label besides the magnifier button, and it is also its aria-label. claimTrue yes: the snapshot records the placeholder foreground #8c8c8c from CSS on #ffffff, at 16px weight 400. I measured the screenshot pixels: the darkest glyph pixel is #8c8c8c on white, 3.36:1. elementFails yes: the live stylesheet refapp-style.css still has '.b-header-slim .b-header-slim-mid-bar-search input[type=text]::placeholder{color:#8c8c8c;font-size:16px}', and the live input sits inside div.b-header-slim and .b-header-slim-mid-bar-search. 16px normal text is not large text, so 4.5:1 applies, and 3.36:1 falls short. message: The placeholder "Buscar serviços, médicos ou informações..." has a contrast of 4.46:1 with the field (#65758b on #f9f9fa). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input type="search" class="flex h-10 w-full border px-3 py-2 text-base ring-offset-background file:border-0 file:bg-transparent file:text-sm file:font-medium file:text-foreground placeholder:text-muted-foreground focus-visible:outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-offset-2 disabled:cursor-not-allowed disabled:opacity-50 md:text-sm pl-10 rounded-xl bg-muted/50 border-border focus:border-blue-400 hover:border-blue-300 transition-colors" placeholder="Buscar serviços, médicos ou informações..." aria-label="Buscar no site" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field (input type=search, aria-label 'Buscar no site', no visible label), whose placeholder is the only visible text saying what the field is for, so it is text that conveys information and 1.4.3 applies. claimTrue: the screenshot's placeholder core pixels are exactly #65758b on a field of #f9f9fa (249,249,250), 14px weight 400, which gives 4.46:1, as stated. elementFails: the live CSS sets ::placeholder to hsl(215 16% 47%) (rgb 101,117,139) on hsl(220 14% 96% / .5) over the white header; every 8-bit rendering of that pair (4.46 to 4.49:1, the WCAG luminance formula works on 8-bit values) is below 4.5:1, and the threshold is not rounded. Only unquantised HSL arithmetic reaches 4.506:1, which no browser renders, so the margin is narrow but the delivered text fails. captureDiffers: the live stylesheet has the same tokens and classes and the screenshot shows a styled page; no difference. The claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header search field (aria-label "Buscar no site") shows the placeholder "Buscar serviços, médicos ou informações..." at 14px, weight 400, and it is the only visible text in the field. In the screenshot the placeholder's solid pixels are exactly #65758b and the field's fill is #f9f9fa (the header behind it is #ffffff), which gives 4.46:1. The live stylesheet agrees: placeholder:text-muted-foreground resolves to hsl(215 16% 47%) = #65758b, and bg-muted/50 is hsl(220 14% 96%) at 50% over white, about #f9f9fa to #f9fafb. Either way the ratio is 4.46 to 4.50, under 4.5:1, and Understanding 1.4.3 says the threshold is not rounded. Reasons I checked and rejected: placeholder text is not exempt (it is not inactive, decorative, invisible or a logotype, and the W3C WAI forms tutorial treats placeholder colour as subject to WCAG's contrast requirement); the aria-label does not change what sighted users have to read; the aria-hidden state and Rampa's hidden overlay come from a dismissible Radix notice dialog ("Atenção, famílias!") that was open at load. Once the dialog is closed, the header looks exactly as captured, and the live bundle has the same classes and theme variables. The margin is small, but it is a failure.

The associated <label for> "Email*" is display:none by the form's CSS, and the snapshot's CDP tree gives Chromium's computed name as "". auditor.rationale: The element is the product-card link a.product-item-link for "Suéter Cashmere Deluxe Gola Alta - Areia" (aria-label and title set to the product name), which wraps the name and the whole price block. claimTrue: the snapshot confirms the installment line sits visually below the Pix price (with the PIX5%OFF badge between) and comes in the DOM right after the final price, but it is not read 'as part of another section': the DOM order is name, final price (with the compare price and discount when on sale), installments, Pix price, PIX5%OFF badge, all inside the same card and the same link; the evidence's on-screen order is also off (the final price is the top price line on screen, as the screenshot shows). elementFails: 1.3.2 asks for a correct reading sequence only where the sequence affects meaning, and F1 needs a CSS layout that changes the meaning. Here the DOM sequence is itself meaningful: the installments follow the price they divide (their total equals the final price) and the Pix price stays next to its PIX badge, so the CSS reordering changes no meaning and the element meets 1.3.2. captureDiffers: the live HTML (curl) has the same price-block markup in the same order and the screenshot shows the same visual layout on every card; the full-page screenshot is taller than the snapshot (more products loaded), which does not touch this claim. False positive: the rule treats a visual/DOM order mismatch as a failure without the change of meaning the criterion requires.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the product-name link of the card for 'Suéter Cashmere Deluxe Gola Alta - Areia'. In the snapshot its children carry CSS order: name 1, price container 2 ('R$799,90 R$1.199,90 - 33 %'), Pix price 3 ('R$759,91'), PIX5%OFF badge 4, installments 5 ('6 x de R$133,32 sem juros'), while the markup goes price, installments, Pix price, badge; the screenshot shows the regular price first, then the Pix price, the badge and the installments last (so the evidence's on-screen sequence, with the Pix price above the regular price, is itself wrong). claimTrue no: the installments do sit visually under the Pix price and after the regular price in the markup, but nothing makes a screen reader read them 'as part of another section': all of it is inside the same link, in the same price block, and the link's name comes from its aria-label, so most screen readers announce only the product name. elementFails no: 1.3.2 applies only when the sequence affects meaning, and F1's test (remove the CSS, check the meaning is unchanged) passes: the markup order reads the regular price, the installments that divide that same price, then the Pix price and its badge, which is at least as meaningful as the visual order; each item stands on its own. captureDiffers no: the live HTML fetched today has the same card markup in the same order with the same classes, and the screenshot matches the snapshot's order values. The rule treats any visual/DOM order mismatch as a failure, a stricter test than 1.3.2.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the footer 'highlight' image, alt 'Image of figure detail for website, mask'. It sits inside a link (href #footerimagetext) that also holds the sr-only text 'See information about Image of figure detail for website, mask', so the image is not the link's only content and R2 does not apply. Activating the link reveals a caption box that is hidden by default (notVisible in the snapshot): 'Netsuke in shape of Noh mask, 18th or 19th century, Japan, CBL J 0193'. claimTrue: the crop and the screenshot show a carved mask, and the alt names a mask. The sentence says the alt describes something the image does not show, which is not so: 'figure detail for website' is CMS filler, not a description of an absent object. elementFails: the alt identifies the subject (a mask), which is the gist that a sighted user gets before opening the caption. The link's name tells users they can get more information, so on a normative reading the image meets 1.1.1, if poorly ('Image of' is redundant and 'figure detail for website' is meaningless). captureDiffers: the footer image rotates on each load. My live fetch of the home page happened to serve this same image with the same alt, the same sr-only text and the same hidden caption, so the capture matches. Label: competent auditors could reasonably fail this alt as placeholder text that leaves out what the object is (a netsuke Noh mask). Read in good faith, the claim would then name that defect, so the label is uncertain rather than false_positive.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 300x300 footer image inside a link (#footer_image > a, href #footerimagetext) that also holds sr-only text "See information about Image of figure detail for website, mask". The link opens a text box captioned "Netsuke in shape of Noh mask, 18th or 19th century, Japan, CBL J 0193". The crop and the screenshot show a carved, grinning mask, which the alternative names ("mask"), so the claim that it describes something the image does not show is false (claimTrue no). elementFails: "Image of ... for website" is CMS wording, but the alternative still identifies the subject. The link's own text gives its purpose, so the image is not the link's only content and H30's control case does not apply. The full identification is one activation away for screen-reader users, just as it is for sighted users, who also see only the picture until they click. The alternative is poor, but it gives what the picture shows, and that meets 1.1.1. captureDiffers: the live footer image rotates on each load (I also got an elephant deity and a man with a spear), but the mask version with this exact alt and caption is still served, so the capture matches a page users receive. auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the Trust Project badge in the footer (img alt "trust project logo", src /footer/trust-project.svg). It is the only content of a link to /about-us/, with no aria-label and no title, so the link's name comes from its contents and is "trust project logo". claimTrue: yes. The link holds only the image, and the alt names the picture (a logo of the Trust Project), not the About Us page. elementFails: yes. I opened the destination: it is "About Us - Birmingham Live", with sections on the editor, ethics, corrections, people, business and diversity. The Trust Project is mentioned there only in passing, twice. Under the R2 test, read as link text, "trust project logo" makes users expect the Trust Project itself (its own site or a page about it), not the publisher's About Us page. H30 requires the alternative of an image that is a link's only content to describe the link's function, and "logo" describes the image. I weighed the counter-reading (the logo shows the text "The Trust Project" and the page carries the publisher's Trust Project disclosures), but the alternative still does not identify the destination. A name like "The Trust Project: about our standards" would keep the visible text and give the destination. The claim names this failure. captureDiffers: no. The live HTML has the identical link, href and alt, and the screenshot shows the badge rendered as captured.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the Trust Project kite-mark image in the footer, the only content of a link to /about-us/ with no aria-label, title or aria-describedby, so the link's name is the alt "trust project logo" (snapshot nameFrom: contents). The claim holds of the capture: the alternative is all the link holds and it says what the picture is (an outside organisation's logo), not where the link goes. I opened the destination: it is "About Us - Birmingham Live", the publisher's own page on its editorial standards, ethics, corrections and people, which mentions The Trust Project in two passing sentences; a user hearing "trust project logo, link" would expect the Trust Project's site or a page about it, not the site's About Us page. The skeptical reading that the Trust Project trust mark conventionally leads to the publisher's standards page does not hold up for users in general, and under the rubric (R2, H30: the alternative of an image that is the only content of a link describes the link's function) neither the visible 'About Us' text link elsewhere in the footer nor anything else cures 1.1.1. The live HTML is identical to the snapshot (same href, alt, no title) and the screenshot is fully styled, so the capture does not differ.

They lead to five non-equivalent pages: New In, Clothing ('Most Wanted Fashion'), Homeware, Accessories and Gift bestsellers. The panels are clipped visually but rendered and exposed in the accessibility tree, so all five are reachable together. A sighted user sees which panel is open (under the highlighted top-level item, beside 'New In X' and 'Shop All X'), so visual information tells them apart: every link of the set fails 2.4.4 by R1. claimTrue: yes, five links, five destinations, nothing in programmatic context differs. captureDiffers: no, the live server HTML has the same menu markup and hrefs, with no aria or nesting. Under R1 every link of the set fails 2.4.4, and the claim (5 links, 5 places, nothing around it tells it apart) is accurate and names that failure. patch.after: Homeware Bestsellers

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: [visual context] The element is 'Bestsellers' in the Homeware mega-menu panel, linking to /homeware/category/bestsellers. The five 'Bestsellers' links in the snapshot are mega-menu items, each alone in its own list item, in panels that are not nested inside the top-level nav list items, with no title, aria-describedby or heading before them (the page has no heading before the footer), so their contexts are identical and they form one R1 set. They lead to five non-equivalent pages: New In, Clothing ('Most Wanted Fashion'), Homeware, Accessories and Gift bestsellers. The panels are clipped visually but rendered and exposed in the accessibility tree, so all five are reachable together. A sighted user sees which panel is open (under the highlighted top-level item, beside 'New In X' and 'Shop All X'), so visual information tells them apart: every link of the set fails 2.4.4 by R1. claimTrue: yes, five links, five destinations, nothing in programmatic context differs. captureDiffers: no, the live server HTML has the same menu markup and hrefs, with no aria or nesting. The claim names this failure: true positive.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: [visual context] This is the Homeware panel's 'Bestsellers' link to /homeware/category/bestsellers. Five links are named 'Bestsellers', one per mega-menu panel: /new-in/best-sellers, /fashion/most-wanted (Clothing Bestsellers), /homeware/category/bestsellers, /accessories/bestsellers and /gift/category/bestsellers. Each sits alone in its list item, the panels are not nested in the top-nav list items (separate meganav-content, no aria-owns/aria-controls), there are no headings in the header and no title or aria-describedby, so their contexts are identical and they form one set. I checked whether the collapsed panels are really exposed: the CDP tree keeps them as non-ignored, focusable links with real bounds (clipped by a zero-height overflow-hidden container, not display:none), and the live HTML serves the same five links, so captureDiffers is no. The destinations are different category bestseller pages (non-equivalent), and a sighted user sees each one only inside the panel opened from its category, beside 'New In <category>' and 'Shop All <category>', which tells them apart. Under R1 every link of the set fails 2.4.4, and the claim (5 links, 5 places, nothing around it tells it apart) is accurate and names that failure. No technique or capture difference holds up: true_positive.

patch.after: Shop all Christmas Gifts

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is hero tile 3's text link 'Christmas Gifts' to /christmas-gifts/all-christmas-gifts, the one link of the set that goes elsewhere. Six links on the page are named 'Christmas Gifts' (top nav, the New In mega-menu image tile, the Gifts mega-menu list item, hero tiles 1 and 3, the footer), none with a title, aria-describedby or preceding heading, so their contexts do not tell them apart. Five go to /christmas-gifts and one, hero tile 3, goes to /christmas-gifts/all-christmas-gifts, so the claim's '6 links, 2 places' holds of the capture (claimTrue yes). I opened both: /christmas-gifts is the Christmas Gifts hub (curated Christmas gift categories, a Christmas gift carousel, a link to All Christmas Gifts) and the other is its full Christmas gift product listing, a child page in the breadcrumb. Both meet the expectation the name 'Christmas Gifts' sets and give the same advertised key content, so they are equivalent resources under R1. Nothing visible tells users that the hero tile leads to a different kind of page either: it is a photo tile labelled 'Christmas Gifts', like the nav item. So the set meets fd3a94 and 2.4.4. captureDiffers: no, the live HTML has the same six links and hrefs. False positive: it counted a different URL as a different purpose (criterion_misapplied).

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is hero tile 3's 'Christmas Gifts' text link to /christmas-gifts/all-christmas-gifts. The snapshot holds six links named 'Christmas Gifts': top nav, the New In mega-menu image tile, the Gifts mega-menu list item, hero tile 1 (white text over the 'COME ON IN' image, not visible in the screenshot) and the footer item all go to /christmas-gifts; only hero tile 3 goes to /christmas-gifts/all-christmas-gifts. None has a title, aria-describedby, sentence, heading before it (the first heading is the footer h2) or parent list item that adds anything, so they form one set; the count '6 links, 2 places' holds and the live HTML serves the same links, so captureDiffers is no. The only non-same pair is /christmas-gifts (the Christmas Gifts landing hub: gift sections, product carousels, edits) against /christmas-gifts/all-christmas-gifts (the full filterable grid of all Christmas gifts). Both cover what a user expects from 'Christmas Gifts'; the ACT glossary allows equivalent resources to differ in amount of information and layout, so I lean equivalent, and nothing visible tells a user that the bookend tile leads somewhere other than the nav or footer link (the photo says nothing about the destination). Others could read the hub and the all-products list as different resources (the site itself labels the latter 'All Christmas Gifts' in its mega menu), so competent auditors would reasonably disagree: uncertain.

patch.after: All Jewellery

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the hero tile's text link 'Jewellery' (/jewellery/all), visible in white over a bracelet photo. Two links are named 'Jewellery': the top-nav item (/jewellery) and a home-page hero tile (/jewellery/all). Neither has a title, aria-describedby or preceding heading, so the context does not tell them apart and they form an R1 set (claimTrue yes: two links, two URLs). I opened both. /jewellery is the Jewellery category hub (h1 'Jewellery', jewellery sub-categories, bestseller and new-in jewellery carousels). /jewellery/all is the 'All Jewellery' product listing, a child page in the breadcrumb. Both give what the name 'Jewellery' advertises, so they are equivalent resources under R1. Nothing visible suggests a different destination either: the tile is a bracelet photo labelled 'Jewellery'. The pair meets fd3a94 and 2.4.4. captureDiffers: no, the live HTML has the same links and hrefs. False positive: it treated a different URL as a different purpose (criterion_misapplied).

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the hero tile's 'Jewellery' text link to /jewellery/all. Two links are named 'Jewellery': the top-nav item (/jewellery, the 'Women's Jewellery' landing page with curated sections and about 72 products) and the hero tile over a bracelet photo (/jewellery/all, the 'All Jewellery' filterable product grid). Neither has a title, aria-describedby, sentence, heading before it or parent list item that adds anything, so they form a set; the claim's '2 links, 2 places' holds and the live HTML is the same (captureDiffers no). Whether this pair fails turns on equivalence: both pages are where a user expects 'Jewellery' to lead, and the ACT glossary lets equivalent resources differ in amount of information and layout, so I lean equivalent; nor does anything visible tell a user the tile leads to a different page than the nav item (the bracelet photo only says 'jewellery'). Others could treat a curated landing page and the full product list as non-equivalent (the site's own mega menu calls /jewellery/all 'Shop All Jewellery'), so competent auditors would reasonably disagree: uncertain.

patch.to: Logos da Lei Rouanet, Lei de Incentivo ao Esporte, ProAC ICMS, CPFL Energia, Instituto CPFL, State Grid e órgãos governamentais.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the sponsor strip image (REGUA-DE-LOGOS-2026.png) between the main content and the footer, with alt="". The crop and screenshot show logos of Lei Rouanet, Lei de Incentivo ao Esporte, ProAC ICMS, CPFL Energia (patrocínio), instituto cpfl and State Grid (apoio), and Governo do Estado de São Paulo, Ministério do Esporte and Ministério da Cultura (realização), with those captions drawn in the image. The snapshot has no text anywhere on the page that names these sponsors or roles, so the claim holds of the capture. The image conveys information (who sponsors, supports and runs the programme), so marking it decorative with a null alt leaves screen reader users without that content: a 1.1.1 failure (situation A, no text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose). The claim names that failure. The live HTML still serves the same img with alt="" and no surrounding text, the same as the capture.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the sponsor logo strip above the footer (REGUA-DE-LOGOS-2026.png) with alt="". The crop and the screenshot show credit labels (patrocínio, apoio, realização) and logos for Lei Rouanet, Lei de Incentivo ao Esporte, ProAC ICMS, CPFL Energia, instituto cpfl, State Grid, Governo do Estado de São Paulo, Ministério do Esporte and Ministério da Cultura. claimTrue: alt="" hides it, and none of this appears in nearby text. The footer text names only the institute's address and links, and the snapshot has no text list of sponsors. elementFails: I looked for a reason it could be decorative and found none that holds. The strip tells users who sponsors, supports and carries out the work (credits that incentive laws require), so it is informative non-text content with no text alternative and no text equivalent nearby. That fails 1.1.1. The claim's summary leaves out some logos and the role labels, but read in good faith it names this failure: informative content hidden by a null alt. captureDiffers: the live HTML has the same img with alt="" in the same place. The two older sponsor images are commented out there, so nothing else supplies the text.

ref: #navigation-desktop-search
subject: pesquise no site
message: The placeholder "pesquise no site" has a contrast of 3.86:1 with the field (#777777 on #eeeeee). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input id="navigation-desktop-search" type="text" class="form-search__input" name="s" placeholder="pesquise no site" required="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the desktop search field in the grey sub-menu bar; its label "Pesquise no site" is visually hidden, so the placeholder "pesquise no site" is the only visible text identifying the field. Sampling the screenshot over the field gives #777777 text on #eeeeee, 3.86:1, and the live stylesheet sets the placeholder colour to #777 inside .header-container--eixos .sub-menu-wrapper on a transparent field over the #eee bar, at 12px bold Montserrat. That is not large text (bold needs 14pt, about 18.7px), so 1.4.3 needs 4.5:1 and the text falls short. Placeholder text is text, not incidental or a logotype, and here it serves as the visible label. The claim states the colours, ratio and requirement correctly. The live HTML and CSS match the capture.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the desktop search field in the grey sub-menu bar. Its only visible label is the placeholder "pesquise no site": the label element has class visuallyhidden. claimTrue: pixels sampled from the screenshot are #777777 glyphs on #eeeeee, which gives 3.86:1, and the text is 12px bold, so not large text. elementFails: I tested the usual escape routes. The live CSS sets the placeholder to color #777 for .header-container--eixos .sub-menu-wrapper .form-search__input, on a transparent background over the #eee bar, so the measure is not a collector artefact. The field is active, so the inactive-component exception does not apply. The placeholder is the only visible label, so it is not incidental text. It falls short of 4.5:1 and fails 1.4.3, and the claim names exactly that. captureDiffers: the live HTML and CSS match the capture (same input, visually hidden label, same placeholder colours), and the screenshot shows the full styled layout.

ref: #portal-searchbox-field
subject: Pesquise em todo site!
message: The placeholder "Pesquise em todo site!" has a contrast of 3.39:1 with the field (#009d8a on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input id="portal-searchbox-field" type="" name="searchword" placeholder="Pesquise em todo site!" class="pesquisa">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Header search field whose placeholder "Pesquise em todo site!" is the only visible text telling what the field is for. Sampling the screenshot gives #009d8a text on #ffffff, 3.39:1, 14px bold (normal size), below 4.5:1. Placeholder text is visible text that conveys information and the field is active, so 1.4.3 applies. The live page (WebFetch got the real server HTML; curl got an F5 bot challenge) holds the same footer, the same news list and the same markup, and the screenshot is a fully styled render, so nothing suggests the capture differs on this point. The claim names this failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header search field #portal-searchbox-field; its placeholder "Pesquise em todo site!" is teal bold 14px on a white pill. My sampling of the screenshot gives #009d8a (and #009889 anti-aliasing) on #ffffff, 3.39:1, below 4.5:1 for non-large text. The obvious skeptic objection, that placeholders are hints outside 1.4.3, does not hold: Understanding 1.4.3 says the criterion "applies to text in the page, including placeholder text", and here the placeholder is also the field's only visible label. The field and its styling are the site's own header, so no capture difference touches it. Fails as claimed.

ref: #pmf-slider > li:nth-of-type(1) > article > a
subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The first carousel slide's image link (a > figure > img alt="Imagem Destacada"). The capture's CDP accessibility tree shows role link with no name, while the img inside is named "Imagem Destacada": Chromium does not take name from content through a figure, so in Chrome and Edge the link is exposed with an empty name, as the claim says. In that sense the element fails 4.1.2 for most users. But the markup is valid and the accessible name computation spec (recursive name from content) would give "Imagem Destacada", which other browsers and axe-core compute, so competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether this is an author failure of 4.1.2 or a user-agent gap. Separately, the image alt fails 1.1.1/2.4.4 for not naming the story. The live HTML is the same, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Slider link . In the capture Chrome's CDP tree gives this link no name, while the sibling card links (a > div > div > img) get "Imagem Destacada ...": Chromium does not take name from content through the figure element, so the claim is true of the capture and of Chrome users. The skeptic reason: by the accname algorithm the figure's descendants are traversed and the name is "Imagem Destacada" (the author used the img-alt-in-link pattern, H30), which Firefox and axe-core's link-name compute; the empty name is a user agent quirk, and with that name the link has a name for 4.1.2 (its poor quality is a 1.1.1/2.4.4 matter). Whether this counts as a 4.1.2 failure turns on accessibility support in Chrome, on which competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so uncertain. Same markup on the live page as far as WebFetch shows.

ref: #main-slider > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a
message: The link text "1" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: bxSlider pager link "1" (href="", the active dot over the featured-news carousel), which shows slide 1. Its text, its name and its context (a pager div with only the numbers, no title, no aria-label; the heading before it is a slide's news headline, hidden) do not tell that it selects a carousel slide, nor which story. Sighted users see the dots over the carousel, so the purpose is not ambiguous to users in general. It fails 2.4.4, and the claim names that. The pager is built by bxSlider in the browser; the live HTML has the same carousel and nothing suggests a different pager.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: bxSlider pager link 1, a dot over the news carousel. Name "1", no title or aria-describedby, generic div ancestors, and the heading just before it is the last slide's h2 about Agefis, unrelated to selecting slide 1. The purpose (show the first slide) cannot be determined from text and listed context, and the dots are not ambiguous to sighted users, so the exception does not apply. Script-generated pager present for users with scripts, as captured. Fails 2.4.4 as claimed.

ref: #top > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(4) > a

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: [visual context] Link "A" (href="#") in the header's accessibility bar, which resets the text size between "A-" and "A+". Its list item holds only "A"; it has no title, aria-label or aria-describedby; no heading comes before it. The visible label "Acessibilidade:" is a neighbouring list item, not context under this rubric, and only the visual A- A A+ pattern tells sighted users what it does, so the purpose is not ambiguous to users in general. It fails 2.4.4, and the claim names that. The live HTML has the same links with no title or aria-label.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: [visual context] Text-size control A (reset to normal size) in li.normal-zoom of the header list "Acessibilidade: A- A A+". Its own list item holds only "A"; there is no title, aria-label or aria-describedby; the list is not nested; no heading precedes it. The "Acessibilidade:" label and the A-/A+ neighbours sit in sibling list items, which the rubric does not count as context. Sighted users understand the A- A A+ pattern, so the ambiguity exception does not apply. Live page (WebFetch) still has the same A-/A/A+ links. Fails 2.4.4 as claimed.

ref: #main-slider > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(1)

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: bxSlider control link "Prev" (href="", shown as an arrow over the carousel), which shows the previous slide. Nothing in its programmatic context (a div holding "Prev Next", no title, no aria-label, the heading before it a hidden slide headline) says it moves a news carousel, and the text is an English abbreviation on a pt-BR page, so I lean to a 2.4.4 failure, as the claim says. But "Prev" does state a direction, and competent auditors often accept previous/next controls of a carousel as having a determinable purpose, so they would reasonably disagree. The control is built by bxSlider in the browser; nothing suggests the live page differs.

skeptic.rationale: bxSlider control Prev for the news carousel. Its name is the English abbreviation "Prev"; no title or describedby; generic div ancestors; the heading just before it is the last slide's h2, which does not name the carousel. The claim's sentence holds for the captured context. But the skeptic reason holds up partly: "Prev" does state the action (go to the previous item), and many auditors accept Previous/Next carousel controls as giving their purpose, while others require "previous slide" and note that an English abbreviation on a pt-BR page is opaque to many users (a 3.1.2 matter, not 2.4.4). Competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so uncertain. Script-generated control, present as captured.
