ref: html > body > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > section:nth-of-type(1) > figure > a > img
message: The text alternative "Logo Branca - Prefeitura Municipal de Fortaleza" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: Footer logo link to "/" (title is empty) holding only the white Prefeitura logo, alt "Logo Branca - Prefeitura Municipal de Fortaleza"; Chrome names the link with that alt. The destination is the home page of the Prefeitura Municipal de Fortaleza portal, and the alt names it: as in H30's example ("Smallville Times" for a linked thumbnail), a link named after the site leads to that site's home, and R2 says an alternative that names the page describes the link's purpose. The "Logo Branca" prefix is noise, not a failure. So the claim that it does not say where the link leads is not true, and the element meets 1.1.1. The live page has the same logo and alt.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Footer logo (crop: white "FORTALEZA PREFEITURA" logo) that is the only content of <a href="/" title="">, the portal's home page. Its alt "Logo Branca - Prefeitura Municipal de Fortaleza" names the Prefeitura whose home page the link opens; read as the link text it lets users tell where the link goes (R2: naming the page suffices; H30's own example uses the destination's name, "Smallville Times"). "Logo Branca" is noise and "home" would be nicer, but neither is a 1.1.1 failure; the logo's text is also covered. Chrome computes this name for the link. The claim that it does not say where the link leads is wrong; the model had the alt and the href and misjudged. Live page has the same alt (WebFetch).

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > footer > div > div > div > section > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(7) > div > img
subject: csm_logo_amb2
message: The text alternative "csm_logo_amb2" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > footer > div > div > div > section > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(7) > div > img

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: Footer image under the h5 'Fliliada a:' (affiliated to): the logo of AMB with the words 'AMB Associação Médica Brasileira', not a link, alt and title 'csm_logo_amb2' (a CMS file name), the same on the live page. The alternative does not describe something absent: 'logo amb' is what the picture is, so the claim's sentence is not accurate. As an auditor I would fail it under 1.1.1 (F30, file name as text alternative; it leaves out the organisation's name that the image shows and wraps the acronym in 'csm_' and '2'). But competent auditors would disagree both on whether an alt that still contains 'amb' fails, and on whether 'describes something the image does not show' names a file-name defect, so the label is uncertain.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Footer image under the h5 "Fliliada a:" (not a link). The crop shows the AMB logo with "Associação Médica Brasileira" beneath it; its alt and title are "csm_logo_amb2", the file's name. Claim: the alt does refer to what the image shows (an AMB logo), apart from the "csm_" prefix and "2" suffix, so "describes something the image does not show" is not accurate as worded. Element: a filename with prefix and suffix noise, where "amb2" is not even the plain acronym, is not a real alternative for the logo (F30). It leaves out the organisation's name, so my lean is that it fails 1.1.1. Still, the alt carries "logo amb" under a "Filiada a" heading, so auditors could reasonably differ on whether it conveys enough, and on whether this claim names the filename defect. Label uncertain. The live HTML has the same alt.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > footer > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > a > img
subject: itarget-icon
message: The text alternative "itarget-icon" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > footer > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > div > a > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: A 30x30 image (a blue swirl logo with no text) is the only content of a footer link to https://itargettecnologia.com.br (the site developer, iTarget Tecnologia), alt and title 'itarget-icon'; the live HTML is the same. Applying R2's first test, the alternative read as the link's text names iTarget, the company whose site the link opens, so it lets users tell where the link goes; it is clumsy and file-name-like ('-icon'), but it does not lose the destination (compare an alt such as 'facebook-icon' on a Facebook link). The claim's second half, that it does not say where the link leads, is therefore not true, and the element meets 1.1.1 on this point (a better alt would be 'iTarget Tecnologia'). The icon lies just below the full screenshot's bottom edge, but the crop and the live page agree with the snapshot.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Footer image link to https://itargettecnologia.com.br (the site developer's credit). subject: A Geriatrics, Gerontology and Aging (GGA), publicação científica oficial da Sociedade Brasileira de Geriatria e Gerontologia (SBGG), agora faz parte da Coleção SciELO Brasil. A inclusão representa uma conquista importante para a revista e para toda a comunidade científica dedicada ao estudo do envelhecimento humano. A novidade amplia as oportunidades de visibilidade, acesso e disseminação das pesquisas publicadas pela GGA, fortalecendo seu compromisso com a ciência aberta e com a produção de conhecimento de qualidade. A entrada na Coleção SciELO Brasil traz benefícios para diferentes públicos envolvidos na produção, na avaliação e na aplicação do conhecimento científico. Para autores e pesquisadores, representa mais oportunidades para que seus artigos sejam encontrados, lidos e citados por pesquisadores do Brasil e de outros países. Para programas de pós-graduação, amplia as possibilidades de divulgação das pesquisas desenvolvidas, contribuindo para sua visibilidade internacional, sem custos adicionais de publicação, conforme as condições destacadas pela revista. Para revisores e editores, reforça o reconhecimento do trabalho essencial da avaliação por pares e do compromisso com a qualidade científica. Para profissionais de saúde e gestores, amplia o acesso aberto a evidências e conhecimentos que podem contribuir para a prática profissional, a organização dos serviços de saúde e a formulação de políticas públicas. Para toda a comunidade do envelhecimento, fortalece a circulação do conhecimento científico, com acesso gratuito para leitores e sem taxas de publicação, conforme informado pela GGA. A inclusão na Coleção SciELO Brasil reforça a missão da GGA de contribuir para o avanço da ciência em Geriatria e Gerontologia e para a disseminação de pesquisas relevantes sobre o envelhecimento. Essa conquista é resultado de um esforço coletivo e representa mais um passo no fortalecimento da produção científica da área, aproximando pesquisadores, profissionais, estudantes e gestores do conhecimento que pode contribuir para um envelhecimento mais saudável. Acesse a GGA e conheça as pesquisas publicadas: Compartilhe essa conquista com orientadores, pesquisadores, estudantes e colegas que contribuem para o desenvolvimento da Geriatria e da Gerontologia.

ref: #colunistas-slide-v3 > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(1)
subject: Previous slide
message: The icon of this button ("Previous slide") has at most 2.60:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#9391bf on #eeeff6). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <button type="button" class="colunistas-prev border-0 rounded-circle" aria-label="Previous slide" tabindex="0" aria-controls="swiper-wrapper-8642b1ed0ef051e2">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: "Previous slide" button of the Colunistas carousel: a 36px round button, background #EEEFF6, holding a Bootstrap Icons chevron. The screenshot shows a thin stroke rendered with subpixel anti-aliasing (pixel pairs #9391BF and #30B0E6; the Next button shows the same pattern from the same colour), so the claim's 2.60:1 is true of the captured pixels. But the authored icon colour is var(--blue) = #0277BD (colunistas-slide-v3.css, .colunistas-controles button; the captured markup has the same colunistas-controles-topo structure), which gives about 4.18:1 against #EEEFF6, above 3:1. Understanding 1.4.11 says to use the colours from the stylesheets rather than the anti-aliased rendering of thin shapes. The button is not disabled. So it passes; the rule measured anti-aliased pixels, a stricter test than the criterion's.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The Colunistas carousel's previous button: a 36px #eeeff6 circle holding a Bootstrap Icons chevron (an icon-font glyph). claimTrue: the snapshot's pixelContrast took the foreground from pixels (foregroundFrom: pixels); in the screenshot the thin stroke is rendered as sub-pixel anti-aliased pairs #9391bf/#30b0e6, so the sentence is true of the captured rendering. elementFails: colunistas-slide-v3.css sets the button's color to var(--blue) = #0277BD on background #eeeff6, which is 4.18:1, above 3:1. Understanding 1.4.11 says to "refer to the colors obtained from the user agent, or the underlying markup and stylesheets, rather than the non-text elements as presented on screen", because thin lines are rendered fainter than their CSS colour, and calls such a case one that nominally passes. Measured that way the icon meets 1.4.11, so the rule applied a stricter test than the criterion. captureDiffers: the live CSS has the same colours; only the static aria-label text differs, which does not touch contrast.

patch.to: Ofertas de Black Friday em eletroportáteis na Pernambucanas. Compre agora.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the image in hero carousel slide 2 of 9. It is the only content of a link to /eletronicos (sorted by price), and the link takes its name from it. Its alt is the placeholder "Descriptive text for the image". The crop shows a Black Friday banner for small appliances ("Todos os eletroportáteis em até 10x sem juros ou 10% off à vista no PIX", "Compre agora"). The alternative names neither the destination nor the offer, so the link's purpose is lost and 1.1.1 fails for a control (H30/G82). The claim says exactly this. Live page: the server-rendered data still holds this slide with the same image and CTA and no alt value, so the capture matches.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the image of hero carousel slide 2 of 9 (the active, visible slide at capture, not aria-hidden). It is the only content of a link to the electronics listing, and the link has no aria-label or title, so its name is the alt "Descriptive text for the image". The crop shows a Black Friday banner for small appliances (10x sem juros or 10% off via PIX, Compre agora). The alt is a placeholder: it describes neither the image nor where the link goes, which fails 1.1.1 under H30 and G82. I looked for a reason it could pass and found none. The live JS bundle hardcodes alt="Descriptive text for the image" in the banner Image component, and the live page config still has this slide active with the same image and URL, so the capture matches what users get (only the slide on screen rotates). The claim names the failure.

ref: #newsletter-email
message: The field "ex.: nome@email.com" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing.

patch.ref: #newsletter-email
patch.before: <input data-fs-input="true" data-testid="fs-input" id="newsletter-email" type="email" placeholder=" " required="" value="">
patch.after: <input data-fs-input="true" data-testid="fs-input" id="newsletter-email" type="email" placeholder=" " required="" value="" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the newsletter field #newsletter-email (type=email, required), labelled by "ex.: nome@email.com", in the form "Não fique de fora das novidades! Preencha com seu email...". It asks for the user's own email address, which is an input purpose listed for 1.3.5. Neither the input nor the form has an autocomplete attribute, so the purpose is not exposed through the HTML autocomplete mechanism (H98). type=email only constrains the format; it does not say that the address is the user's own. The live page renders on the client, so I could not see its markup, but the newsletter section config is unchanged and offers no autocomplete option. Nothing suggests a difference from the capture.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Newsletter signup field (id newsletter-email, type=email, required, label "ex.: nome@email.com", under the heading "Não fique de fora das novidades!"). It collects the user's own email address, a purpose in WCAG's Input Purposes list, and has no autocomplete attribute. I checked whether anything could make it pass. type=email gives only the data format, not that the address is the user's own, and the sufficient technique H98 relies on the autocomplete token. In the live JS bundle, the CustomNewsletter component renders this input with id, type, required and label but no autoComplete, while other forms in the same bundle set autoComplete:"email". So the live page matches the capture. The claim names the 1.3.5 failure.

message: The link text "Confira" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

patch.ref: #__next > section:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a
patch.before: <a data-fs-link="true" data-fs-link-variant="display" data-fs-link-size="regular" data-testid="fs-link" data-fs-popup-banner-image-link="true" target="_self" aria-label="Confira" href="/colecao-completa">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the only control besides Close in a modal popup with aria-label "Live Sawary Jeans". It is an image link to /colecao-completa, the full product listing. aria-label="Confira" ("check it out") sets its name, and the banner image inside has alt="". The image shows a different offer: 10% OFF EXTRA on the first purchase over R$79,99 with coupon BEMVINDO10, "APROVEITE". "Confira" says nothing of the destination. The link has no title or description, no sentence or list item, and no heading before it; a dialog's name is not in the rubric's context list. Even if "Live Sawary Jeans" counted, it names another campaign. 2.4.4 fails, and the claim names this. The popup is not ambiguous to users in general, since sighted users see the offer. Live data still has the PopupBanner (imageOnly, same image, alt "", title "Live Sawary Jeans", CTA "Confira" to /colecao-completa), shown once per session. The empty alt on a text image is also a 1.1.1 issue.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: [visual context] The element is the whole-banner image link inside the popup dialog "Live Sawary Jeans". ref: #newsletter--email__sections--29148651618637__footer

message: The placeholder "Email" has a contrast of 4.30:1 with the field (#72716d on #000000). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input id="newsletter--email__sections--29148651618637__footer" class="newsletter__form__input" type="email" name="contact[email]" placeholder="Email" value="" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the footer newsletter email field with placeholder 'Email'. The snapshot's pixel measurement records #72716d on #000000 (4.30:1), so the sentence holds for the capture. But the capture was taken with the newsletter pop-up open: the screenshot shows the pop-up and a cookie dialog over a dimmed page, and the accessibility tree marks the page as ignored behind an active modal dialog. The footer uses the theme's secondary_scheme, where the placeholder rule .newsletter .newsletter__form__input::placeholder sets color: var(--color-form-text) = #e5e3db on --color-form-background #000000, about 16:1. #72716d is exactly #e5e3db at 50% under a black backdrop (the header search box measures the same way, #767573 for #eceae6), so the measured colour is the modal backdrop, not the text. A user sees the footer at full contrast once the pop-up closes, and content behind an open modal is not what 1.4.3 judges. The element meets 1.4.3; the false positive comes only from the capture.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The footer newsletter field's placeholder 'Email'. The snapshot measured #72716d on #000000 (4.30:1) from pixels, so the sentence holds for the capture. The live CSS, though, sets .newsletter .newsletter__form__input::placeholder to var(--color-form-text), which is #e5e3db in the footer's secondary_scheme, on a #000000 form background. subject: for=search
message: 3 elements have id="search": this label names the first of them, not the field beside it. Give each field a unique id.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the sr-only label '"Search"' (for="search") in the desktop header search form. The snapshot and the live HTML both have three inputs with id="search" (a hidden one in the header, the visible desktop one, the search overlay's), and the first one gets all three labels, so the claim holds for the capture: this label names the hidden first input, not the field beside it. On 4.1.2, though, the visible field still has a programmatically determined name. HTML-AAM's name computation for input type=search falls back to the placeholder, here 'Search', the same word as the label, so screen readers announce it as Search and the ACT form-field-name rule passes. The duplicate id is a markup defect (4.1.1 Parsing in WCAG 2.1, which W3C now treats as always satisfied for HTML), but it leaves the field with no missing name or role, so 4.1.2 is met. The rule treats the broken for/id reference as a 4.1.2 failure without checking the name the field ends up with.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The sr-only label for="search" in the desktop header search form. The page does have three inputs with id="search", in both the snapshot and the live HTML. The first is the mobile nav search (lg:hidden), so all three labels name it and the visible desktop field beside this label gets no name from it. The claim is true of the capture. However, for 4.1.2 the desktop field still has a programmatically determined name: its placeholder 'Search' is used for the accessible name by HTML-AAM and browsers. ACT rule e086e5, which maps to 4.1.2, lists a placeholder-named input as passing. That name says the same as the label would. The label is not a UI component itself. The duplicate id is F77, a WCAG 2.1 4.1.1 Parsing failure, not a 4.1.2 one, so the checker applied the wrong criterion.

The snapshot records #777777 on #f5f5f5 (4.107:1), and pixels sampled from the screenshot over the item are exactly #777777 and #f5f5f5, so the claim holds. The live style sheets still set .breadcrumb{background-color:#f5f5f5} and .breadcrumb>.active{color:#777}, and the live HTML has the same breadcrumb, so the capture matches what users receive. The live CSS is Bootstrap's '.breadcrumb>.active{color:#777}' on '.breadcrumb{background-color:#f5f5f5}'; the theme's white-background override only targets '.region-content>ol.breadcrumb', and this breadcrumb sits in '.region-main-first', so the grey background seen in the screenshot is what users get. #777777 on #f5f5f5 is 4.11:1, below 4.5:1, and no exception applies (it is ordinary text, not a control, logo or incidental text). That describes the topic as 2.4.2 asks, so the claim that it says nothing about the page is false. The live page returns the same title.

ref: #block-views-block-bloco-de-pagina-inicial > div > div > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > p:nth-of-type(2) > a
message: The link text "Clique aqui" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link 'Clique aqui' goes to https://site.mppr.mp.br/sic ('SIC - Serviço de Informações ao Cidadão | MPPR'). It ends a paragraph that reads 'Bem-vindo ao canal de comunicação direta entre o Ministério Público do Paraná e o cidadão. Aqui você encontrará as principais informações de interesse público sobre a instituição e poderá fazer pedidos de acesso à informação.' That same paragraph is programmatically determined context, and it tells users the link opens the channel for public-interest information and access-to-information requests, which is what the SIC page is. The bold title link above it is in a separate paragraph, so it does not count, and it is not needed. The claim that nothing around the link tells where it goes is false of the capture. The live HTML has the same markup. The other 'Clique aqui' links are in different paragraphs, so R1 does not apply. The link passes 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link 'Clique aqui' goes to https://site.mppr.mp.br/sic and ends the paragraph 'Bem-vindo ao canal de comunicação direta entre o Ministério Público do Paraná e o cidadão. Aqui você encontrará as principais informações de interesse público sobre a instituição e poderá fazer pedidos de acesso à informação.' That paragraph is the link's programmatically determined context, and it describes the destination: the destination, 'SIC - Serviço de Informações ao Cidadão | MPPR', opens with nearly the same welcome text. Link plus paragraph tells users the link leads to the channel for access-to-information requests, so it meets 2.4.4, and 'nothing around it does' is false. The other 'Clique aqui' links on the page sit in different paragraphs, so R1 does not group them with this one. The live page has the same markup.

ref: #block-views-block-bloco-de-pagina-inicial > div > div > div > div > div > div > p:nth-of-type(5) > a
message: The link text "Clique aqui" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link 'Clique aqui' (title 'Clique aqui') goes to the Ouvidoria Contato page. Its own paragraph reads 'Horário de atendimento ao público: Clique aqui.', under the h3 'Nossos contatos', so the link text together with its paragraph tells users the link shows the public opening hours. The destination does exactly that: its first content is 'Horário de atendimento ao público: De segunda à sexta-feira, das 12h às 19h'. The claim's 'nothing around it does' is false of the capture, which held that paragraph (with the full stop oddly moved to the front). The live HTML has the same paragraph and link. The other 'Clique aqui' links on the page sit in different paragraphs, so R1 does not group them. The link passes 2.4.4, and the model had the context and judged wrongly.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link 'Clique aqui' (title also 'Clique aqui') goes to /Ouvidoria/Pagina/Contato. It sits in the same paragraph as the bold label 'Horário de atendimento ao público:', under the h3 'Nossos contatos'. A paragraph is programmatically determined link context, so link plus paragraph reads 'Horário de atendimento ao público: Clique aqui', meaning 'see the public service hours'. The destination opens with exactly that ('Horário de atendimento ao público: De segunda à sexta-feira, das 12h às 19h'), so the purpose can be determined (G53). 'Nothing around it does' is false of the capture, and the packet gave the model this paragraph. The live page has the same markup.

ref: #block-celeparheader-2 > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > h1
message: The heading "OUVIDORIA-GERAL DO MINISTÉRIO PÚBLICO" says nothing about the content under it.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the page's only h1, the site logo heading, whose name is 'OUVIDORIA-GERAL DO MINISTÉRIO PÚBLICO' (sr-only) plus the visible 'Ouvidoria-Geral do Ministério Público'. This page is the Ouvidoria-Geral home page, and everything under the heading (the Ouvidoria navigation, 'Quem somos' about the Ouvidoria, its contacts and other service channels) is about the Ouvidoria-Geral, so the heading describes the topic of the content it introduces. The doubled text is redundant, but it does not make the heading non-descriptive. The claim that it says nothing about that content is false of the capture. The live HTML has the same h1. The heading passes 2.4.6.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The h1 is the header logo: screen-reader text 'OUVIDORIA-GERAL DO MINISTÉRIO PÚBLICO' plus a home link 'Ouvidoria-Geral do Ministério Público'. This page is the Ouvidoria-Geral's home: the content under the heading is the Ouvidoria-Geral navigation, 'Quem somos' ('A Ouvidoria do Ministério Público do Paraná é um canal...'), the forms for filing and checking complaints, and the Ouvidoria's contacts. The heading names the very body the page is about, so it describes the topic as 2.4.6 asks, and 'says nothing about the content under it' is false. Repeating the name inside the heading is redundant but is not a 2.4.6 failure. The live page is the same.

ref: #block-views-block-bloco-de-pagina-inicial > div > div > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > span > div > div > picture > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the grey 'i' speech-bubble icon (the Brazilian Lei de Acesso à Informação symbol) beside the 'Serviço de Informação ao Cidadão (Lei de Acesso à Informação)' entry. It is not inside a link (confirmed in the live HTML). Its alt 'ícone Acesso à Informação' accurately names what the icon stands for. The image is redundant with the adjacent text, but the alternative is meaningful, not a placeholder like 'spacer' or 'image' (F39), so it serves an equivalent purpose and does not fail 1.1.1. The live page has the same image and alt.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the grey speech-bubble 'i' icon of the Access to Information service, with alt 'ícone Acesso à Informação'. It is not inside a link: in both the live HTML and the snapshot it is span > div > picture > img, with no anchor. Next to it is the strong link 'Serviço de Informação ao Cidadão (Lei de Acesso à Informação)'. The alt correctly identifies what the icon stands for, so it serves the same purpose as the image. Being redundant with the adjacent text is at most a best-practice point: the icon is a recognisable service symbol, not pure decoration, so F38 does not clearly apply. It meets 1.1.1, and Rampa was right to report nothing. The live page is unchanged.

ref: #block-celeparfooter-2 > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the footer logo, the coat of arms with the words 'Ministério Público do Estado do Paraná', and it is the only content of a link to https://mppr.mp.br/ (the MPPR portal home). Its alt 'Ministério Público do Estado do Paraná' reproduces the text in the logo and names the link's destination, as H30 asks, so the image passes 1.1.1. The live HTML has the same link, image and alt. The cookie banner covers it in the screenshot, but the crop shows the logo.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The footer logo image (coat of arms with 'MINISTÉRIO PÚBLICO do Estado do Paraná') is the only content of a link to https://mppr.mp.br/, the MPPR home page (destination title 'Ministério Público do Estado do Paraná'). Its alt 'Ministério Público do Estado do Paraná' gives the text in the logo and names the destination, which meets H30. It meets 1.1.1, and Rampa was right to report nothing. The live page is the same.

ref: #block-views-block-bloco-de-pagina-inicial > div > div > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > span > a > div > div > picture > img
message: The text alternative "ícone CNMP" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The image (a 'CN MP' logo tile) is the only content of a link to https://www.cnmp.mp.br/portal/, the portal of the Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público. Its alt 'ícone CNMP' names CNMP, the destination's organisation, so with the image replaced by its alternative (the G82/R2 test) users can tell the link goes to CNMP. The word 'ícone' is redundant, but the alternative identifies the destination as H30 asks. The claim's 'does not say where the link leads' is therefore false of the capture. The live HTML has the same link and alt. The image passes 1.1.1 on this point.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the CNMP logo icon, alt 'ícone CNMP', and it is the whole content of a link to https://www.cnmp.mp.br/portal/ (accessible name 'ícone CNMP', both in the snapshot and in the live HTML). The destination is the portal of the Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (title 'Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público - Início'). By R2's first test, read as the link's text, the alternative names the destination's organisation, CNMP, which the strong link 'Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP)' right beside it spells out. Users can therefore tell where the link goes, and it passes 1.1.1 on this point, however redundant the word 'ícone' is. So 'does not say where the link leads' is false: the alternative does name it. The live page matches the capture.

ref: #block-views-block-bloco-de-pagina-inicial > div > div > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > p:nth-of-type(1) > strong > a

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link text 'Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP)' goes to https://www.cnmp.mp.br/portal/ ('Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público - Início'). The link text alone names the destination, and no other link on the page shares this name, so it passes 2.4.4. In the snapshot it carries target=_blank and an empty invisible span, which a script adds; the served HTML lacks them, but neither touches 2.4.4. (A new window opening without warning is not a 2.4.4 matter.)

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link text 'Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público (CNMP)' goes to https://www.cnmp.mp.br/portal/, whose title is 'Conselho Nacional do Ministério Público - Início'. The text alone names the destination. No other link on the page shares this name, so R1 does not apply (the image link and the 'Clique aqui' beside it go to the same address under other names). The empty 'element-invisible' span adds nothing, and target=_blank is not a 2.4.4 matter. It meets 2.4.4, and Rampa was right to report nothing. The live page is the same.

ref: #wpforms-2430-field_1
message: The field "Email *" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing.

patch.ref: #wpforms-2430-field_1
patch.before: <input type="email" id="wpforms-2430-field_1" class="wpforms-field-medium wpforms-field-required" name="wpforms[fields][1]" placeholder="Deixe aqui o seu melhor e-mail" spellcheck="false" aria-errormessage="wpforms-2430-field_1-error" required="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The newsletter field under 'Fique por dentro das novidades' ('Inscreva-se em nossa newsletter...'). It is an input type=email with the hidden label 'Email *' and the placeholder 'Deixe aqui o seu melhor e-mail', so it asks for the user's own e-mail address, which is one of the listed input purposes. Neither the snapshot DOM nor the live raw HTML has any autocomplete attribute on it (the live page has no autocomplete attribute at all). type=email gives the data type, not the purpose. No H98 autocomplete token means the purpose cannot be programmatically determined, which fails 1.3.5. The claim names exactly that. The live markup is identical to the capture, so captureDiffers is no.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the newsletter sign-up field under 'Fique por dentro das novidades': label 'Email *', placeholder 'Deixe aqui o seu melhor e-mail'. It collects the user's own e-mail address, one of the input purposes WCAG 2.1 section 7 lists. The input has type="email" but no autocomplete attribute, both in the snapshot and in the live HTML (the live page has no autocomplete attribute anywhere). type="email" gives the data format, not the purpose, and is not a sufficient technique for 1.3.5; H98 (autocomplete="email") is. I found no technique on the page that makes the field pass, and the capture matches the live markup. The claim names exactly this failure.

ref: #masthead > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > button
subject: Abrir pesquisa
message: The icon of this button ("Abrir pesquisa") has at most 2.85:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #999999). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <button type="button" class="heg-search-trigger" aria-label="Abrir pesquisa" aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="heg-search-1">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header's search button: a white magnifier icon (search.css forces color and stroke #fff) on a transparent background over the hero slider. claimTrue: the snapshot's pixel record for this icon says #ffffff on #999999, 2.849:1, so the sentence matches what the capture recorded. But #999999 is the hero widget's CSS background colour (post-15.css, .elementor-element-de1bb59 {background-color:#999999}), which the hero photo (RRM_9905-2-scaled.jpg, same file live and in the snapshot) covers completely. At the icon's position users get the photo's dark blue sky. I rebuilt the cover-fitted photo at 1265x711 and sampled about #2d435a under the icon, roughly 10:1 against white. The snapshot itself measured #29435a from pixels behind the 'Ensino e Pesquisa' menu text in the same header row, and the blur and 90% brightness filter only darken it. When the header gets its #0079DA background, white is about 4.6:1. Either way it is above 3:1, so elementFails is no. captureDiffers: the saved screenshot shows a dimmed 'ATENÇÃO!' notice over the icon, not #999999. The pixel record the rule used therefore comes from a render state users never see. So it is a capture/collector error, not a real low-contrast icon.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The search button is transparent and shows only a 23px magnifier. The plugin CSS (heg-pesquisa search.css) forces the stroke to #fff and the background to transparent. It sits in the header, which is absolutely positioned and transparent, on top of the hero slider. #999999 is exactly the background-color the slider widget sets in CSS (post-15.css, .elementor-element-de1bb59), so it shows only where the hero photo is not painted. The capture's full-page screenshot does show the photo painted, but the button's area is covered there by the 'ATENÇÃO' popup (navy #061a30 and grey text), so no #999999 sits next to the icon in the capture: claimTrue no. The live page has one hero slide (RRM_9905-2-scaled.jpg, a photo that is already darkened). Mapped onto the 1280x720 hero, it puts dark blue sky behind the icon. White against those pixels gives at least 9.4:1 (about 10:1 median), well above 3:1, so the icon passes 1.4.11. The header is not sticky, so the icon never sits over other content. The rule measured a render without the photo, a loading state that is not the page users receive, so this is a collector error.

ref: #nossas-unidades > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3)
subject: Próximo slide
message: The icon of this button ("Próximo slide") has at most 1.80:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ededede6 on #edeff2…#acaeb2). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The 'Próximo slide' arrow of the 'Nossas Unidades' image carousel: an Elementor swiper button that shows only a chevron in Elementor's default hsla(0,0%,93%,.9) (#ededede6), with no background or border, drawn over whichever photo is rightmost in the autoplaying carousel. The snapshot's pixel record behind it (#e4e4e6, #edeff2 to #acaeb2) matches the light area of the CEPEP photo, white coats and a grey table. I sampled that spot of the CEPEP photo in the screenshot (#c7c9cd, #a7a9ad, #e8e7ea, #f1f3f4): 1.04 to 2.0:1 against the chevron. On light slides like this one and the white hospital facades, the only visual indicator of the control falls below 3:1 and nearly disappears, which fails 1.4.11. In the saved screenshot the chevron sits on a brick wall, where most of it passes, but the carousel rotates through the failing states for every user. The live page has the same carousel, images and default arrow styling, so captureDiffers is no.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'next slide' arrow of the 'Nossas Unidades' Elementor carousel: a div with role=button that shows only a 26px chevron. The colour is Elementor's default hsla(0,0%,93%,.9), i.e. #ededede6; post-15.css changes only its font-size. Nothing contrasting sits behind the chevron, so it is drawn straight on the photos. The carousel autoplays every 5 s (live data-settings), so the photo behind the arrow changes. The snapshot's pagination has slide 1 active, while the screenshot shows a later position with the Rede Feminina photo at the right. The capture therefore holds two different moments, and the rule's sample (#edeff2…#acaeb2, at most 1.80:1) cannot be checked against the screenshot: claimTrue cannot_tell. In the screenshot, the upper half of the chevron sits on a dark red wall (5 to 10:1). The lower half sits on a light sidewalk and grass: half of the pixels under and around the arrow are below 3:1, down to 1.04:1, so the chevron's shape does not reach 3:1. Light parts of other slides make it worse. No technique, such as a contrasting backing shape or outline, makes it pass. The live page has the same arrow, colour and nine photos. It fails 1.4.11, and the claim names that failure: low contrast between the icon and what is behind it.

ref: #page > div > div:nth-of-type(16) > div > div > div > div > div > article:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: A 'Ler Mais' button-styled link in the third news card, pointing to the article 'Solidariedade à mesa: Ópera de Bambu realiza caranguejada Solidária...'. Under this round's context rule, the heading just before the link counts. In document order that heading is the card's own h3, whose text is exactly the article's title (and is itself a link to the same URL). With that heading, the link's purpose can be determined. The other 'Ler Mais' links on the page each sit under their own article h3, so their contexts tell them apart and they do not form an R1 set. It meets 2.4.4, and Rampa was right not to report it. The live page has the same card markup (h3 link, excerpt, 'Ler Mais' to the same URL), and the screenshot shows it, so captureDiffers is no.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'Ler Mais' button-link in the third news card, an article element. Just before it in the same article is the h3 'Solidariedade à mesa: Ópera de Bambu realiza caranguejada Solidária para apoiar o Hospice Erasto Gaertner'. Under this rubric the preceding heading counts as context (H80), and with it the link's purpose, reading that story, is clear and matches the destination. The other two 'Ler Mais' links on the page each come after a different h3 and lead to their own stories, so their contexts tell them apart and they do not form an R1 set. The live page has the same three cards with the same addresses. The link meets 2.4.4, so Rampa was right to report nothing.

ref: #menu-item-1840 > div > a

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The top-level 'Ensino e Pesquisa' item of the main menu: a link with href='#' inside a role=button container. The accessibility tree exposes it as collapsed with a popup menu. Its submenu holds 'Ensino e Pesquisa' (/ensino-e-pesquisa-2/), 'CEPEP' and 'Estudos em Recrutamento'. Its purpose is to open the Ensino e Pesquisa submenu, which its name plus the expanded and has-popup state convey, so 2.4.4 is met. The submenu link with the same name sits in its own nested list item, under a parent list item that is the top-level item (H81), and only the top-level item has the toggle state. Their contexts tell them apart, so they do not form an R1 set. The accessible name also carries a Font Awesome private-use glyph (U+F107), which is noise but does not hide the purpose. Possible role issues (a link used as a toggle, a control nested in a role=button) fall under 4.1.2, not 2.4.4. The live markup is identical to the capture.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the top-level menu link 'Ensino e Pesquisa' (href="#", aria-haspopup, collapsed). It opens the 'Ensino e Pesquisa' submenu, which holds Ensino e Pesquisa, CEPEP and Estudos em Recrutamento. Its text and its popup and collapsed states make the purpose clear: it opens that section's menu. One submenu link has the same name and goes to /ensino-e-pesquisa-2/. Its context differs, though: it has its own list item, nested under the parent list item (H81), whereas the trigger is the parent item itself. So the two do not form an R1 set, and the trigger does not navigate anywhere. The live markup is the same. The link meets 2.4.4, so Rampa was right to report nothing.

ref: #colophon > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > ul > li:nth-of-type(8) > a
message: The link text "Qualidade" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Visita Benchmarking - Hospital Erasto Gaertner".

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: A footer 'Links Úteis' link named 'Qualidade' that leads to /visita-benchmarking/. The destination's title and h1 are 'Visita Benchmarking', as the packet says. But I opened the page, and its first content section is a video banner whose heading (h2) is 'Qualidade'. The banner is followed by 'VISITAS INSTITUCIONAIS', guidance for benchmarking visits, a 'Processos de qualidade' (JCI) document and a visit-request form. So it is the hospital Quality area's page, and it presents itself as 'Qualidade'. There is no other quality page on the site (/qualidade/ returns 404). The link text matches the heading the destination displays, which describes its purpose. Understanding 2.4.4 does not require the document's title. So the 'does not match' part of the claim does not hold, and the link meets 2.4.4. Rampa read only the destination's title, h1 and description, so it missed the banner heading. The live footer link and the destination match the capture's records (same href, title and h1).

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is a link in the footer's 'Links Úteis' list: text 'Qualidade', leading to /visita-benchmarking/. I opened the destination live. Its title and its h1 'Visita Benchmarking' (in the theme's page header) match what Rampa recorded, so the page seems unchanged. Its visible banner heading, an h2 over a background video, reads 'Qualidade'. The page describes institutional benchmarking visits run as part of the hospital's quality work, links to 'Processos de qualidade' (the JCI booklet) and lists 'Escritório da Qualidade' among its services. The link text is the destination's own visible heading and topic, and Understanding 2.4.4 does not require the page's title to be used. The purpose can be determined from the text, so the link passes. The claim's title is accurate, but 'does not match' is not. Rampa read only the title and h1 and missed the 'Qualidade' banner heading, so the cause is missing context. The live footer link is unchanged.

ref: html > body > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(5) > label
subject: Continue lendo
message: The text "Continue lendo" has at most 4.24:1 contrast with what is behind it (#007ae8 on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The 'Continue lendo' label, which expands the article. The live CSS (.read-more: color #007ae8, white background, font-size 1.2rem = 19.2px, font-weight 600) and the screenshot confirm the measurement: #007ae8 on #ffffff is 4.24:1, so the sentence holds for the capture. Whether 4.5:1 or 3:1 applies depends on whether 19.2px (14.4pt) at weight 600 is 'bold' for WCAG's large-scale threshold of 14pt bold. Open Sans is not loaded (no @font-face), so the text falls back to the system sans-serif (Arial, Helvetica, Roboto), and none of these has a 600 face. Browsers then render the Bold face, and in the screenshot the text is visibly bold. Read that way, the text is large scale and 4.24:1 passes the 3:1 requirement, which is my lean. But WCAG gives no numeric weight for bold, and axe and many auditors only count computed weight 700 or more as bold, which would fail it at 4.5:1. Competent auditors would split on this, so the label is uncertain.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'Continue lendo' label that expands the article. The live CSS matches the capture: .article-html .read-more has color #007ae8 on the white page, font-size 1.2rem (19.2px, 14.4pt) and font-weight 600; #007ae8 on #ffffff is 4.24:1, so the sentence's numbers are true of the capture. The skeptic's reason: 19.2px is above 14pt, and the page asks for 'Open Sans, sans-serif' without loading any web font, so on a typical machine the fallback (Arial/Helvetica, which have only regular and bold faces) renders weight 600 with the bold face, as the screenshot shows clearly bold text. Bold text of at least 14pt is large-scale text under WCAG, whose threshold is 3:1, which 4.24:1 meets. WCAG gives no numeric definition of bold, and tools split on 600 (Chrome DevTools counts 600 as bold, axe-core requires 700), so competent auditors would reasonably disagree; my own lean is that the element passes, hence uncertain rather than a true positive. No capture difference: same colours, size and weight on the live page, and the button is shown by default (checkbox unchecked).

ref: html > body > a > div:nth-of-type(1)
subject: ACESSE NOSSO CANAL NO ZAP
message: The text "ACESSE NOSSO CANAL NO ZAP" has at most 3.98:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #007bff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (it partly covers other elements). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The 'ACESSE NOSSO CANAL NO ZAP' text in the fixed floating WhatsApp-channel link at the bottom right. auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The WhatsApp share link under 'Compartilhe:'. The live CSS gives it a #24c34b circle, and the screenshot pixels show only #ffffff and #24c34b: a white WhatsApp glyph on green. That is 2.34:1, and the green circle against the white page is also 2.34:1, so the claim is true of the capture and the page. The icon is the WhatsApp brand mark in roughly its brand colours (WhatsApp's own white on #25D366 is even lower). Understanding 1.4.11 says logos are exempt from the contrast requirements. For logos that act as controls it gives only best-practice advice, and it removes the exemption only when a logo that normally has enough contrast is shown low-contrast by author choice, which is not the case here. My lean is that it passes on that reading. But the normative user-interface-component bullet has no essential or logo exception, and many auditors fail brand-coloured icon-only share buttons under G207. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so the label is uncertain. Separately, the link has no accessible name, which fails 4.1.2 and 2.4.4, not this criterion.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the WhatsApp share link under 'Compartilhe:': a 35px circle with background #24c34b holding a white (fill #fff) WhatsApp glyph, no text. White on #24c34b is 2.34:1, and the green circle against the white page is also 2.34:1, so the glyph that tells users which network the control shares to has under 3:1 against every adjacent colour; under the normative text of 1.4.11 that is a failure, and the sentence is true of the capture. ref: #edit-email
message: The field "E-mail" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #edit-email
patch.before: <input data-drupal-selector="edit-email" pattern="[a-z0-9._%+-]+@[a-z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]{2,4}$" type="email" id="edit-email" name="email" value="" size="60" maxlength="254" class="form-email required form-control" required="required" aria-required="true">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the required E-mail input in the footer "Sign up for MFA Mail" form, labelled by a visible "E-mail *" label. It collects the user's own email address, which is an Input Purpose (email) under 1.3.5, but the input has no autocomplete attribute. type="email" and name="email" do not identify the purpose of the field as the user's email address (H98 uses autocomplete). The snapshot records Chromium's form issue FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError on this field, so the claim's last sentence is true as well. The live HTML has the same input, still with no autocomplete. The field fails 1.3.5, and the claim names exactly that failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The footer 'Sign up for MFA Mail' field (input type=email name=email, visible label 'E-mail') asks for the visitor's own email address, a purpose in WCAG's Input Purposes list (email). It has no autocomplete attribute in the snapshot or in the live HTML, and Chromium flagged it (formIssues: FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError), so both sentences of the claim are true. I looked for a reason it could pass: type=email gives only the data format, not that the address is the user's own, and name=email is not a mechanism WCAG recognises. So the purpose cannot be programmatically determined (H98 not met), and the field fails 1.3.5 for exactly the reason the claim gives.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > header > nav:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > form > div:nth-of-type(1) > label
subject: for=edit-search
message: 2 elements have id="edit-search": this label names the first of them, not the field beside it. Give each field a unique id.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the visually hidden <label for="edit-search">Search</label> in the desktop header search form. The page has two inputs with id="edit-search": a hidden one in the mobile menu (#navbarSupportedContent) and the desktop one beside this label. The snapshot's labelControl shows that this label points at the first, hidden input, so the claim is true of the capture. But 4.1.2 asks for a programmatically determined name, and the field beside the label has one: Chromium's accessibility tree names it "Search" (nameFrom: placeholder, from placeholder="Search"). That passes F68's test, which checks the browser's accessibility tree for a name that is not empty. Its role (searchbox) and value are exposed too. The wrong label target is a markup defect (duplicate IDs, which the WCAG 2.1 errata treat as always satisfied under 4.1.1). Whether a placeholder alone is enough as a label is a 3.3.2 question, not a 4.1.2 failure. The live HTML has the same two ids and both labels, so the capture matches. The rule treats the misassociated label as a 4.1.2 failure without checking that the field has a name from another source, which is stricter than the criterion.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the visually hidden label for="edit-search" of the header search form. The claim holds of the capture: two inputs have id="edit-search" (live HTML has the same duplicate, from a mobile-menu copy and a header copy), the label's for resolves to the first, hidden one, and Chrome's tree shows this label unattached (LabelText, empty name). But the visible field beside it still gets the accessible name 'Search' from its placeholder (ax nameFrom placeholder), the same text the label carries, and its role and value are exposed. Duplicate IDs fail 4.1.2 only when they break a name, role or value relationship (the old 4.1.1 issue, always satisfied for HTML in WCAG 2.1 as amended); here nothing is lost, because the label is invisible anyway and the name is unchanged. Not a 4.1.2 failure: the rule treats the duplicate id itself as the failure.

ref: #edit-email
message: The field "E-mail" only accepts a set format (pattern="[a-z0-9._%+-]+@[a-z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]{2,4}$"), and nothing on screen explains it.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the required E-mail input of the footer newsletter form. It has the visible label "E-mail *" and pattern="[a-z0-9._%+-]+@[a-z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]{2,4}$". The screenshot shows only the label, the field and a Submit button, with no format instructions, so the claim is true of the capture. The live HTML is the same. The label states the expected data, an email address, which is a customary format, so in my reading 3.3.2 is met. However, the pattern rejects valid addresses with uppercase letters or top-level domains longer than four letters. When that happens the browser shows only "Please match the requested format", which is better treated under 3.3.3. Understanding 3.3.2 says instructions may specify formats "if there are specific rules for correct input", and some auditors log undisclosed format restrictions under 3.3.2. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree on whether this restriction requires an on-screen instruction, so the label is uncertain.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Of the capture the sentence holds: the newsletter field has pattern="[a-z0-9._%+-]+@[a-z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]{2,4}$" and no on-screen hint (live HTML identical, form without novalidate, and the page's scripts only use native validity). But on the page users receive, the pattern constrains nothing: browsers compile pattern with the v flag, where an unescaped '-' in a character class is a syntax error (verified in V8: 'Invalid character in character class'), so the element has no compiled pattern and accepts any address type=email accepts. The field has a visible label 'E-mail' with a required marker, which identifies the expected input in its customary format. 3.3.2 needs no further instruction here: the finding demands one for any pattern attribute, which is stricter than the criterion.

ref: #header-search
subject: Search for hampers...
message: The placeholder "Search for hampers..." has a contrast of 2.50:1 with the field (#42404280 on #ececec). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input id="header-search" class="search__input w-full input js-search-input" type="search" role="combobox" name="q" placeholder="Search for scarve" autocomplete="off">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field. Its visible prompt is the placeholder, which cycles through 'Search for throws/hampers/scarves...'; the visible label is hidden. The live CSS (main.css) sets .search__input::placeholder to rgba(var(--text-color)/.5), with --text-color 65 64 66 and --search-bg-color #ececec in the header style. That blends to about #969697 on #ececec, which is 2.50:1. The darkest placeholder pixel in the screenshot is #979697 on #ececec (2.495:1). Placeholder text is visible text and fits none of the 1.4.3 exceptions (not inactive, not decorative, not incidental), so at 16px/400 it needs 4.5:1 and fails. The claim states the colours and ratio correctly; at capture the attribute held 'Search for scarve' mid-animation, but every placeholder string uses the same style. The live page has the same input and CSS, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header search field (input type=search, role combobox, name 'Search') whose placeholder a script cycles through 'Search for throws...', 'Search for hampers...' and 'Search for scarves...' (the data-placeholder attributes; the capture caught it mid-typing as 'Search for scarve'). claimTrue: yes. The quoted string is one of the cycled placeholders, and the colours hold: the live main.css sets .search__input::placeholder to the text colour at 50% alpha, and the screenshot's placeholder pixels are #979697 on #ececec, 2.49:1, at 16px normal weight. elementFails: yes. The placeholder is the only visible text saying what the field is for (the 'Search' label is not shown), so it is not incidental, and 2.49:1 is below 1.4.3's 4.5:1. I found no technique or exception that would make it pass. captureDiffers: no. The live HTML and CSS give the same placeholder strings and the same placeholder colour rule.

ref: #titulopesquisa
message: The label "Localizar" does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header's site search box: placeholder 'Localizar', aria-label 'Título do Curso', followed by a magnifier button whose Filtrar() sends the text to /busca (a Google site search). In WCAG's definition, a label is the text presented to all users. Here that is 'Localizar' ('Find') on a field paired with a search button, which describes the field's purpose (search the site) as 2.4.6 and G131 require. 2.4.6 does not require the label to spell out the input format. claimTrue is no: in that setting, 'Localizar' does tell users to type what they want to find. The claim demands a stricter, instruction-like label. The aria-label 'Título do Curso' is a leftover that misnames the field for assistive-technology users. That is the accessible name, not the presented label, so it is a 2.5.3 Label in Name / 4.1.2 concern rather than 2.4.6, and the claim does not point at it anyway. aria-describedby points to a missing id 'basic-addon2'. The live HTML is identical to the snapshot. The element does not fail 2.4.6: false_positive.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header search box: <input placeholder="Localizar" aria-label="Título do Curso"> followed by a magnifier button that submits to /busca, a Google custom site search (h2 "Busca"). The claim is not true of the capture: the field's label (accessible name) is "Título do Curso"; "Localizar" is only the placeholder. And "Localizar" next to a search button does describe the purpose (find on the site), which is all 2.4.6 asks; saying what exactly to type is a 3.3.2-type instruction, so the model applied a stricter rule than 2.4.6 requires. The field does fail 2.4.6 for another reason the claim does not name: its programmatic label "Título do Curso" (course title) describes a purpose the field does not have, since it searches the whole transparency site, which has no course catalogue (this also touches 2.5.3, visible "Localizar" not in the name). Live HTML today has the same attributes as the snapshot, so no capture difference. Because the element fails only for a reason the claim does not name, the label is false_positive.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The placeholder "Busca" in the header search field. The theme's style.css sets input[type=text] color to --cor-texto-medio (#949494), and ::placeholder inherits it (#949494 on focus as well). The field has no background of its own and sits on the white header (--cor-background: white), and its font is 14–16px at weight 400. #949494 on #ffffff is 3.03:1, below the 4.5:1 that 1.4.3 asks for normal text. The placeholder is the field's only visible label, so it is not incidental. The screenshot crop shows light-grey "Busca" on white, and the live CSS matches.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Placeholder "Busca" in the header search field. The theme's live style.css sets input[type=text] color to --cor-texto-medio #949494 and ::placeholder to inherit (and #949494 on focus), with no background, so it sits on white; the screenshot's darkest glyph pixels are exactly #949494 on #ffffff, 3.03:1, at 14px normal weight (the 801-1420px media query sets --fonte-pequena to 14px), so 4.5:1 applies. Skeptic checks: the placeholder is the field's only visible label, so it is information-bearing text and no 1.4.3 exception (incidental, logotype, large text) applies. The page offers an "Alto Contraste" toggle that turns the field white on black, but G174 holds only if the alternate version conforms to all success criteria, and the same DOM in that mode keeps failures such as the alt="Imagem da página" images (1.1.1), so it does not rescue the default presentation. The snapshot exposes it as an image with no name, so assistive technology gets nothing from it. That is the sense in which the claim calls it hidden: it is not aria-hidden. It is also not keyboard-operable, which is a 2.1.1 issue. main.js shows the banner whenever the 'privacy' cookie is absent, so first-time visitors get it just as the capture did. The claim names the real failure.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the full-width hero banner, an image that is the only content of a link to /lp/vivara-gisele-bundchen, with alt 'Campanha Natal Fashion'. The image shows Gisele Bündchen with the text 'FEITA NO BRASIL, COM ALMA BRASILEIRA' and 'EXPLORAR'. The destination (fetched live) is titled 'Lançamentos: Novas joias, novas histórias' and shows the new collections (Harmonia, Sopro, Seixos, Ritmo, Bamboo). 'Campanha Natal Fashion' is an internal campaign label that appears nowhere on screen. It names neither the destination nor the banner's text, so it fails H30/G82: when an image is all a link holds, its alternative must give the link's function. Per R2, 1.1.1 fails and the claim names that failure. The live home page has the same banner image, alt and href.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the full-width hero banner, the only content of a link to /lp/vivara-gisele-bundchen. The crop and screenshot show Gisele Bündchen with the text "FEITA NO BRASIL, COM ALMA BRASILEIRA" and "EXPLORAR". The alt is "Campanha Natal Fashion", and the live homepage data still has it (promotionId banner_home_vivara_lancamentos_gisele_brillare). The skeptic case I tested: the destination's CMS name is "Vivara - Campanhas - Gisele - Natal", so "Campanha Natal" matches an internal label. But nothing a user perceives uses that name. The destination's title is "Lançamentos: Novas joias, novas histórias", the banner's visible text is about "made in Brazil" and "explore", and "Fashion" appears nowhere. The alternative neither identifies the destination (the Gisele / new-releases page) nor conveys the text in the image (H30, G94). The link has no title and no other content. By R2, a 1.1.1 claim that such an alternative does not say where the link leads is a true positive.

patch.after: <input data-fs-input="true" data-testid="fs-input" type="email" required="" class="emailField" placeholder="E-MAIL" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the newsletter sign-up field ('Acompanhe nossas novidades / Cadastre seu e-mail'), <input type="email" required class="emailField" placeholder="E-MAIL">, with no autocomplete attribute. It collects the user's own e-mail address, which is the 'email' purpose in the Input Purposes list, and type="email" only sets the data format, not that the value is the user's address, so 1.3.5 is not met (H98 would add autocomplete="email"). The claim states exactly this. The live site's client bundle renders the same input (type email, required, className emailField, placeholder E-MAIL, no autocomplete), so the capture matches what users get.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the footer newsletter field ("Acompanhe nossas novidades / Cadastre seu e-mail"): input type="email", required, placeholder "E-MAIL", with no autocomplete attribute in the snapshot HTML. The live site's JS bundle (chunk 3635) renders the same input (type email, required, className emailField, placeholder E-MAIL, no autoComplete), so the capture matches what users get. I looked for reasons it might pass. The field asks for the user's own address to subscribe them, so it is information about the user, and "email" is one of the listed Input Purposes. type="email" only gives the data format: it does not say the address is the user's own, and it is not the sufficient technique (H98, autocomplete). No other mechanism identifies the purpose. The claim names exactly this failure.

ref: #regionalization-cep
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <input data-fs-input="true" data-testid="fs-input" id="regionalization-cep" type="tel" placeholder="Informar um CEP" data-fs-regionalization-form-input-cep="true" data-fs-regionalization-form-input-cep-error="false" inputmode="numeric" name="regionalization-cep" value="">

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the CEP field of the regionalization modal: <input id="regionalization-cep" type="tel" placeholder="Informar um CEP">, with a <label for="regionalization-cep">CEP</label> that is not rendered (display:none; Chrome marks it notRendered). In the capture, Chrome's AX tree gives the textbox the name "" with a labelledby relation to that hidden label. The modal and the input were rendered at capture time, with bounds and live AX nodes, so the claim that the browser computes no name is true of the capture. In Chrome the control exposes no name, which matches F68 ('does not have a name exposed to assistive technologies'), so I lean towards fail. But HTML-AAM falls back to the placeholder once the hidden label yields nothing, which gives the name 'Informar um CEP'. axe and ACT-style tools would pass it, and NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver announce the placeholder. Competent auditors would reasonably split between a 4.1.2 failure and a 3.3.2-only placeholder-as-label issue, hence uncertain. I could not compare with the live page: the modal and its CSS are client-rendered in a lazily loaded chunk that a plain fetch does not return.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the CEP field (#regionalization-cep, type tel, placeholder "Informar um CEP") in the open regionalization modal dialog. It has a <label for="regionalization-cep">CEP</label>, but the label is notRendered in the snapshot. Chromium's own accessibility tree in the capture gives the textbox name "" (relation labelledby to the hidden label, no fallback to the placeholder). Rampa's spec-style name "CEP" differs from the browser's. I checked that this is not a collector artefact. The live CSS (chunk 07555f5c2a623e33) has "[data-fs-regionalization-form-input-cep-container] [data-fs-input-field] [data-fs-label]{display:none}", and the live JS (chunk 9450) renders the same input with label "CEP" and placeholder "Informar um CEP", so users get the same hidden label. Two skeptic points I weighed: the accname spec allows hidden native labels, and the placeholder may be announced as a description. Neither gives the control a name in the browser's accessibility tree. F68's test reads the browser's accessibility tree, so 4.1.2 fails. Saying a screen reader says only "textbox" may overstate it, since the placeholder can be read as a description, but the claim names the real defect: no computed name.

ref: #__next > section:nth-of-type(9) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3
message: The heading "LIFE" says nothing about the content under it.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is an h3 'Life' (shown as LIFE) heading one of the footer link columns, next to 'Joias Vivara', 'Nossa Empresa', 'Atendimento' and 'Informações'. Its links (Aliança de Namoro, Pingentes, Pulseiras, Brincos, Piercings, Brinco Masculino, Corrente Masculina) all go to /life/... categories. Beside the 'Joias Vivara' column, the heading tells users the column lists Life brand categories, so it describes its section and 2.4.6 is met. The claim that it says nothing about the content is false. The live footer configuration (CustomFooterV2) has the same 'Life' title and links.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the h3 "Life" (shown uppercase) at the top of a footer column. Every link under it goes to the Life by Vivara sub-brand: Aliança de Namoro, Pingentes, Pulseiras, Brincos, Piercings, Brinco Masculino and Corrente Masculina, all on /life/... addresses. The column next to it is headed "Joias Vivara" for the main brand. Life is a brand that the page itself names ("Visite também" Life logo, "Encontra a Vivara e Life", "Life by Vivara" in the consent text). So the heading names the topic of its section, Life-brand categories, and 2.4.6 does not require a longer heading. The live homepage data has the same footer column (title "Life" with these submenu items).

ref: #__next > section:nth-of-type(4) > div > nav > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(9) > div > div > button > a > img
message: The text alternative "Imagem de Colares" leaves out what the image conveys here.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the product photo in the 'Colares' tile of the 'NAVEGUE POR CATEGORIA' carousel (an active, aria-hidden=false slide). It sits inside a link whose name, 'Ver categoria Colares', comes from aria-label (title 'Colares'), next to the visible text 'Colares'. The crop shows a single gold-and-pavé collar necklace, there only to illustrate the necklace category. The alt 'Imagem de Colares' gives that purpose: the 'Imagem de' prefix is redundant, and an empty alt would have been better because the link is already named, but a description of this particular necklace is not needed for a category illustration. 1.1.1 is met, so the claim that the alternative leaves out what the image conveys here is false. The live HTML has the same markup (aria-label, title, alt).

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the thumbnail of the "Colares" tile in the "NAVEGUE POR CATEGORIA" carousel. The crop shows a single gold collar necklace on a grey background, a representative product photo for the category. It sits inside a link with aria-label "Ver categoria Colares" and title "Colares", next to the visible text "Colares". The aria-label sets the link's name, so the alt does not even feed into it. In this context the image only illustrates the category. "Imagem de Colares" says it shows necklaces, which is the information that matters; the details of this particular necklace are not needed for an equivalent purpose. The "Imagem de" prefix is redundant but not a failure. The live SSR HTML has the same link and alt. Nothing in the image is left out that the context needs, so the claim does not hold.

ref: #__next > section:nth-of-type(5) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(3)
message: The link text "MONTE SEU PORTA-JOIAS" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Joias Essenciais: Clássicos Atemporais em Ouro, Prata e Diamantes | Vivara".

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the whole third card of the three-card section, a link to /lp/vivara-joias-classicas with aria-label 'MONTE SEU PORTA-JOIAS'. Its content is the card heading h3 'JOIAS ESSENCIAIS', the line 'Escolhas que transformam o visual do dia-a-dia' and the CTA 'MONTE SEU PORTA-JOIAS'. The destination is titled 'Joias Essenciais: Clássicos Atemporais em Ouro, Prata e Diamantes', a catalogue of essential pieces. 'Monte seu porta-joias' ('build your jewellery box') is an ordinary shopping invitation to pick pieces for one's collection, and the link's own text, which this rubric counts as context, names the destination outright ('JOIAS ESSENCIAIS'; the site menu uses the same label for this address). The name and its context therefore describe the purpose, and Understanding 2.4.4 does not require the page title to be repeated. The claim that the text does not match the destination is false. Rampa had both the card text and the destination title. The live page has the same card data and the same destination title.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the third card link of the three-card section. Its aria-label is "MONTE SEU PORTA-JOIAS", the same as its visible call to action. Its content is the image (alt "JOIAS ESSENCIAIS"), the h3 "JOIAS ESSENCIAIS" and "Escolhas que transformam o visual do dia-a-dia". It leads to /lp/vivara-joias-classicas, titled "Joias Essenciais: Clássicos Atemporais...". "Monte seu porta-joias" (build up your jewellery collection) is a fitting call to action for a landing page of essential everyday pieces to buy, so the text does not contradict the destination. The link's own text, which this round counts as context, names "JOIAS ESSENCIAIS", the destination's title. The h3 inside the link also stays in the accessibility tree, because links do not have presentational children. So the purpose can be determined from the link text and its context. The live homepage data has the same card (cardCta label MONTE SEU PORTA-JOIAS, href /lp/vivara-joias-classicas, cardTitle JOIAS ESSENCIAIS). The model had the link's content and the destination title and still judged it a mismatch.

ref: #footer > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(6) > figure > a > img
subject: Safe to create
message: The text alternative "Safe to create" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: #footer > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(5) > div:nth-of-type(6) > figure > a > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The image is the 'We support Safe to Create' badge (an Irish arts-sector initiative), the only content of a link that opens the festival's Dignity-At-Work-Policy.pdf. Its alternative, 'Safe to create', names the initiative. It does not identify the destination, the festival's Dignity at Work policy as a PDF: a user would expect information about Safe to Create. Under H30 and R2, an image that is all a link holds needs an alternative that describes the link's function. Replacing the image with 'Safe to create' (G82) does not tell users that they will open the policy document. So the link fails 1.1.1 for the reason the claim gives. The link has no title, and the live HTML has the same href and alt, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Footer logo image (the 'We support Safe to Create' badge, alt 'Safe to create') that is the only content of a link to https://www.wexfordopera.com/content/files/Dignity-At-Work-Policy.pdf. I read the PDF: an 11-page Wexford Festival Trust 'Respect and Dignity at Work Policy (Bullying & Harassment)', in which Safe to Create appears only as one short section saying the Trust is a signatory. The alt describes the badge, not the control's function: a user hearing 'Safe to create, link' would expect the Safe to Create initiative, not the Festival's own policy document as a PDF. I looked for reasons it might pass: there is no title, no text in the link, and per R2 and H30 a 1.1.1 control alternative must identify the destination, which this one does not (its loose thematic link to the policy does not name the document). claimTrue yes, elementFails yes, and the claim names exactly this failure. The live HTML has the same link and alt, so captureDiffers is no.

ref: #header > div > div > a:nth-of-type(1) > img:nth-of-type(1)

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the header logo image (Wexford Festival Opera wordmark with the '75' anniversary mark) inside the link to the homepage. The link also holds a mobile copy of the logo that is hidden at desktop width, and the browser computes the link's name as 'Wexford Festival Opera'. An alternative that names the organisation, for a logo linking to its home page, describes the link's function (the H30 pattern), and the decorative '75' mark does not need to be in it. The element meets 1.1.1. The live HTML has the same two images with the same alt, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header logo image (alt 'Wexford Festival Opera') inside the brand link to the home page https://www.wexfordopera.com/, whose title is 'Wexford Festival Opera 15-31 October 2026'. The alt gives the organisation's name, which is both the text shown in the logo and the name of the destination, so per H30 it describes the link's function; the '75' anniversary numerals are branding and leaving them out does not lose the purpose. The second logo image in the same link is display:none at desktop width (marked hidden in the snapshot), so the link is not announced twice. The live HTML matches the snapshot, so captureDiffers is no. No 1.1.1 failure: no missed issue.

ref: #footer > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > figure > a > img
message: The text alternative "Investors in Diversity Bronze" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

The alt names the accreditation scheme the destination runs, so read as link text it tells users they will reach the Investors in Diversity (Bronze) accreditation's site; by R2's first test (the alternative names the subject or product of the destination) and H30 it describes the link's purpose, so claimTrue is no and elementFails is no.
