ref: #footer > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(7) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(1)
message: The link text "IT" could mean several things here.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: [visual context] This is the footer link 'IT' to the Italian welcome page (benvenuti-al-festival-dellopera-di-wexford). It has no title, aria-label, aria-describedby, lang or hreflang, and it sits with 'FR' and 'DE' in a flex div that is not a paragraph, list item or table cell. The nearest heading before it is 'Get our newsletter', which says nothing about it. So under this round's context list, its purpose must come from 'IT' alone, and on an English page 'IT' is ambiguous: it could mean Italian or Information Technology. Only the visual grouping with the FR and DE links shows sighted users that these are language links, so the link is not ambiguous to users in general and the exception does not apply. The element fails 2.4.4 by the rubric's fixed context rule, and the claim names that ambiguity. The live HTML matches the snapshot, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Footer link 'IT' to the Italian welcome page (benvenuti-al-festival-dellopera-di-wexford), the first of three bare links 'IT FR DE' in one flex div, with no lang, hreflang, title or aria-label and no visible 'Language' label (screenshot and live HTML agree with the snapshot, so captureDiffers is no). The skeptic's reason against the claim: 'IT' sits in the same run of text (an implied paragraph in HTML terms) as 'FR' and 'DE', and that trio reads as a set of language codes, so link text plus context lets users work out that it opens the Italian version; on that reading the element passes and the claim that it could mean several things here is not true of the capture. But the rubric's context list names sentences, paragraphs, list items and table cells, and a bare div of links is not clearly any of them; read strictly, 'IT' alone (which a screen reader may voice as the word 'it') does not give the purpose, while sighted users can infer it from the visual cluster, which would make it a failure. Competent auditors split on bare language-code switchers under 2.4.4 (some file them under 3.1.4 or best practice), so the label is uncertain although my own answers lean to a pass.

ref: #primary > li:nth-of-type(5) > a
message: The link text "Our story" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the top-level 'Our story' item of the main navigation: an a with href='#' and data-bs-toggle='dropdown', with a chevron, that opens the Our story submenu (Explore the festival, Our history, About and so on). In the capture the submenu is hidden, so its list item reads only 'Our story' and no visible heading comes before it. That part of the claim holds. But the text names the section the control opens, which is its purpose: users can tell that it leads to the Our story part of the site. So the claim that the text does not tell where it goes is wrong, and the element meets 2.4.4. It shares its name with the breadcrumb 'Our story' link, but the breadcrumb's own context ('Home > Our story > Contact us') and the toggle's list item tell them apart, and the toggle opens a menu rather than leading to another resource; R1 does not make it fail. The real defect is a 4.1.2 one: a link role with no aria-expanded on a control that works as a menu button. The live HTML matches the snapshot, so the capture does not differ.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'Our story' item of the primary navigation: an <a href="#" data-bs-toggle="dropdown"> with a chevron that opens the 'Our story' mega-menu (panel-our-story, with 'Our roots, our journey and our work today' and links such as Our history, Our archive, Contact us). Its purpose is to open that section's menu, and the text 'Our story' names the section; a top-level navigation item named after its section is conventional and determinable from the text alone, and its list item holds the submenu it reveals. The claim that the text does not tell where it goes and that nothing around it does is therefore not true of the capture (the listitem context in the packet holds the submenu), so claimTrue is no and elementFails is no. That it is a link with href="#" acting as a disclosure button is a 4.1.2 name/role/state matter, not 2.4.4. The live HTML and the screenshot match the snapshot (captureDiffers no).

ref: #block-admissions2020-languageswitcher > ul > li > a
subject: Español
message: "Español" is in Spanish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="es" to the link.

patch.ref: #block-admissions2020-languageswitcher > ul > li > a
patch.after: <a href="/es" class="language-link" aria-label="Español" lang="es">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the language-switcher link to /es, whose aria-label and visible text are "Español". Neither it nor any ancestor has a lang attribute, so it inherits the page's lang="en". The only lang="es" in the live HTML is an hreflang on a head link element, which does not set the language of the text. This is exactly Understanding 3.1.2's "Alternative language links" example, where each link names the language in that language and carries lang. The word is not a proper name or an English vernacular word, so the exceptions do not apply. The live markup matches the capture, and the claim names the failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the language-switcher link to /es whose name (aria-label) and visible text are "Español", inside a page with lang="en"; neither the link nor its span carries a lang attribute in the snapshot or in the live HTML. claimTrue: yes. elementFails: yes. I looked for an exception: Understanding 3.1.2 treats exactly this case in its example "Alternative language links" (link text is the language's name in that language, and its language is indicated with a lang attribute), so neither the proper-name nor the single-word exception applies, and the hreflang alternates in the head do not set the link's language. captureDiffers: no, the live page is unchanged on this point. True positive.

ref: #block-admissions2020-content > article > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2)
subject: region keydown
message: This element ("Hero image carousel") takes keyboard focus and listens to keydown, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as region, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.
html: <div class="hp-hero--slideshow slider-image" role="region" aria-label="Hero image carousel">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the hero carousel container. The live page's inline script deliberately sets tabindex=0, role=region and aria-label "Hero image carousel" on it, plus a keydown handler that moves to the previous or next slide on Left/Right Arrow. The capture shows the same focusable region with a keydown listener, so the claim's facts are true of the capture. But the element does not fail 4.1.2. It has a programmatically determined name and a WAI-ARIA role, and region is the role the ARIA Authoring Practices carousel pattern gives a carousel container. F59 fails only elements with handlers that have neither a native role nor a fitting ARIA role. Arrow keys here are an extra shortcut on a container; the slide functions are exposed as separate native buttons (Slide 1-6, Play and Pause). A button or link role, as the claim suggests, would misrepresent the container. Treating every focusable element with a keydown listener as a control that needs a widget role is stricter than the criterion.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the hero slideshow container, a div given tabindex 0, role region and aria-label "Hero image carousel" by the page script, which also binds ArrowLeft/ArrowRight to previous/next slide. claimTrue: yes, it is focusable, has a keydown listener and is exposed as a named region with no widget role. elementFails: no. Its role and name are programmatically determined, and region is the role the ARIA carousel pattern gives a carousel container; the carousel's actual controls are native buttons (Play and Pause, and the Slide 1 to 6 dot buttons), so nothing is operable only through this div. Arrow keys on a focused named region are a convenience comparable to scrolling a focusable scroll region, not a div posing as a button or link, which is what F59 describes; the suggested fix (make it a button or link) would misrepresent it. captureDiffers: no, the live HTML and inline script set the same attributes and handler. The rule applied a stricter reading than 4.1.2 requires.

ref: #block-admissions2020-main-menu > ul > li:nth-of-type(4) > button > svg
message: The text alternative "Down Arrow" is all its button holds, and does not say what the button does.

ref: #paragraph-2144 > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
message: The text alternative "Image Collage." describes something the image does not show.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the large image beside the "Belonging - Find Community, Support and Collaboration" text, with alt "Image Collage. ". The crop and the screenshot show it really is a collage: photos of UCLA students, a dancing student, a Bruin bear drawing, and notes reading "UCLA", "LOS ANGELES" and "WE ARE Sooo BACK". So as worded, the claim that the alternative describes something the image does not show is false. Still, the alternative names only the image format and conveys none of what the image shows (diverse students, Los Angeles, the "we are back" message), so it is not an equivalent and fails 1.1.1. If the image were judged decorative, a non-null alt like this would fail too (F39). Per the rubric's good-faith reading, an alternative said to describe something the image does not show, when it leaves out most of what the image conveys, names the real defect. The live HTML still has alt="Image Collage. ".

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the Belonging blade image (belonging.jpg) with alt "Image Collage.". claimTrue: no, the crop and screenshot show the image is in fact a collage (students, a UCLA logo, a bear mascot, and pasted text "Los Angeles" and "We are sooo back"), so the alternative does not describe something absent. elementFails: yes on either reading, since "Image Collage." is placeholder-like: if the image is informative it leaves out what the picture conveys, including its text (F30-type), and if it is decorative beside a heading and paragraph that carry the message, it should have a null alt (F39, alt="image"). ref: #block-lgd-languageswitcher--2 > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
subject: Gaeilge
message: "Gaeilge" is in Irish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="ga" to the link.

patch.ref: #block-lgd-languageswitcher--2 > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
patch.after: <a href="/ga" class="language-link" hreflang="ga" data-drupal-link-system-path="<front>" lang="ga">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The language switcher link "Gaeilge" is the Irish name of the Irish language, on a page whose html element has lang="en". Neither the a element, its li nor its ul carries a lang attribute, in the snapshot and in the live HTML alike; hreflang="ga" describes the linked page, not the language of the link text. Understanding 3.1.2 treats a single word as part of the surrounding language unless a change of language is clearly intended; here it is, since the endonym is offered to Irish speakers, and an English voice does not pronounce it the same. It is not a proper name carried across languages untranslated (English says "Irish"), so no exception applies: the word's language is not programmatically determined (H58 not met). The claim names this failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The language switcher link "Gaeilge" (href /ga, hreflang="ga") has no lang attribute and inherits lang="en" from the html element, both in the snapshot and in the live HTML; hreflang describes the destination, not the link text. I looked for an exception: the word is not a proper name of a person, place or brand, and it is not English vernacular that an English synthesiser pronounces correctly, and a change of language is plainly intended. Understanding 3.1.2 gives this exact pattern as its "Alternative language links" example, with lang on each language link. The element fails 3.1.2 and the claim names that failure.
